utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sabbah, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is IT-05-87-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this a Pre-Trial Conference in the case of the Prosecutor against Milan Milutinovic and five co-accused. The Bench for the trial is now composed, as you see of myself, as Presiding Judge, and Judge Chowhan and Judge Kamenova, and when the trial commences we will be joined by a Reserve Judge, Judge Nosworthy. May I now take the appearances for the various parties today. And please give a full account of these appearances because it seems to me that once that's done, then it need not be done on a regular, daily basis, unless you feel the need to introduce some new personality to the Court. So I'll start with the Prosecutor. And if there are personnel that you expect to be here on a regular basis -- who are not here today, you could perhaps mention that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Tom Hannis. I'm one of the two Senior Trial Attorneys on this case. To my right is Mr. Chester Stamp, who is the other Senior Trial Attorney on this case. And, Judge, for the duration of the trial, most days either Mr. Stamp or I will always be here. There may be some exceptions, but that's the general rule. To Mr. Stamp's right is Susan Grogan, our case manager. She'll be here every day, we hope. Behind me the gentleman you see is Mr. Mathias Marcussen, one of our Trial Attorneys. Next to him is Christina Moeller, another Trial Attorney. In addition, Your Honour, we have several other Trial Attorneys who may be appearing occasionally for witnesses. I can give your their names right now, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's probably better, I think, for all of us if they are just appearing on certain later occasions just to tell us at the time, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do that at that time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Slodoban Zecevic. I am counsel for Mr. Milan Milutinovic. In the court Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan as a lead counsel will be appearing. Unfortunately, he was tied up today in another case, so he will be joining us this afternoon. To my left is Ruzica Jovanovic, our legal assistant, and to my right is Srdjan Mujanovic, our case manager. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Just a moment, Mr. Fila. Mr. Boas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Toma Fila. I am Mr. Nikola Sainovic's lead counsel. To my right is my co-counsel, Attorney-at-Law, Vladimir Petrovic. He will represent Mr. Sainovic together with me. And to my left is Attorney-at-Law Mirko Mrkic, our legal assistant. Thank you. No one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Team of three?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Team of three, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Tomislav Visnjic. I am represent General Ojdanic. To my left is Mr. Norman Sepenuk, and to my right is Suzana Zivkovic, our case manager. Also, the Defence team will be joined at certain stages of these proceedings by Mr. Peter Robinson, our legal adviser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, I am Mr. Aleksander Aleksic, Attorney-at-Law from Belgrade. I am counsel for Mr. Pavkovic. Our lead counsel, Mr. Ackerman, is absent today unfortunately and will be absent throughout this first week. Aleksandar Vujic, our case manager, will be joining us in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have details of Mr. Ackerman's illness. I understand the position entirely, and we will at some stage this morning be discussing the trial arrangements to try and cause as little difficulty as possible for the conduct of the Defence case of Mr. Pavkovic in the absence of Mr. Ackerman. Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning. I am Mihajlo Bakrac, lead counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic. I am joined today by Mr. Milos Cvijic, our case manager. For the time being, I am unable to say who else might be joining us. Nevertheless, yesterday we heard that the issue of our co-counsel would probably be resolved in the course of the next week. I will be informing you in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Branko Lukic, I am the lead counsel for General Lukic. With me today is Mr. Ivetic, my co-counsel, and Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic, who is our legal assistant. Occasionally we will be joined by our fourth member, Mr. Boris Zorko. So that's the composition of our team for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're fighting fit today, Mr. Lukic, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've recovered. Thank you. Well, I don't guarantee to follow the agenda which was issued to you, but we'll try to follow it as far as possible, and there are a few matters we can get through, I think, fairly quickly. There's a number of outstanding motions. One of these is at the instance of the Prosecution for admission of documentary evidence prior to the stage at which any of that evidence might be referred to by witnesses. There have been intervening orders of the Trial Chamber requiring further submissions. The Prosecution's further submissions have now been received. There is a fairly imminent deadline, I think, for Defence responses. And that motion will probably be dealt with in writing by a written judgement following the receipt of these responses. I imagine, however, that it will be sometime into August before that decision is issued, and certainly not before the trial resumes after the recess. There's reference on the agenda to a Prosecution Rule 92 bis motion. That's historical, really, because the decision in that has already been issued. Yesterday there was a hearing in the application of -- on behalf of Mr. Lukic under Rule 54 bis for a binding order against the Government of the Republic of Serbia now. I expect the decision on that to be issued today, and I indicated in broad terms at the end of the hearing yesterday what the terms of that decision would be. There's a further motion at the instance of Mr. Lukic which is entitled a motion to compel Prosecution disclosure. My understanding of that motion, however - which remains outstanding - is that the solution to the problem was probably the release into the e-court system of the documents. Now, that's largely complete, but it's only been completed I think possibly in the course of this morning, but it's very recently completed -- as far as the release of the Prosecution documents is concerned. Now, Mr. Lukic, can you tell me if that solves the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of our problems is that we don't have an access to the intranet and e-court. And the other problem is that I think that I don't know how would it work because I haven't seen it yet what has been released, but what we received from the Prosecution is not possible to follow. I think that it will be hard for them to find their own document in that bunch of documents we received from them because what we opened -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. What we opened is a hundred documents, and then we have to try to find among those hundred documents which one you need, because there is no corresponding number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I am beginning to understand the problem. It's taken me some time - through probably technophobia rather than anything else - to try to get to grips with this problem. But I'm assured that the job of linking your inquiry to the right document should be made easier once the documents are downloaded, or uploaded, whichever the technical term is, into the e-court library. And that has only now happened. So I think what I would ask you to do is to see if it does, in fact, improve the situation. Now, has your e-court training still to be done, is that the difficulty, or has it been done and you just haven't got the proper link to the system?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The training is completed, but we don't have a log-in on the system yet. So maybe we should wait until tomorrow or until the day -- until Monday to see whether we would be able to log-on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that the communication on this subject has not been terribly satisfactory. The Chamber's own staff have been trying to get responses, I think mainly dealing with Mr. Ivetic, and have had some difficulty getting responses from him. Now, I think we ought to pin down when this is going to be finally resolved. I don't want something like this as a running sore through the trial. So can we invite you to let the Chamber know the position by Wednesday of next week so that we've still got time next week to address it if it remains a problem, and you've got time at the beginning of the week to see if you can solve the problem. The gentleman who did the e-court training will be in court at the beginning of next week, and he's accessible today also. So it would be your responsibility or whoever in your team is dealing with this to make contact with him, resolve the problem of access, and see if in fact this does make it possible to do the job that you found difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not saying, by the way, that even if it doesn't the motion will necessarily be successful, but it makes a difference obviously to how we approach the motion, to know just how difficult the access problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you again. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I come now to the first of the fairly substantial issues, and that is the Prosecution's proposed expert list. There are five expert witnesses that no one takes exception to so far as relevance is concerned or so far as qualifications are concerned, and there are five others to whom objection on both these grounds is taken. It's not -- it doesn't automatically follow that because no objection on these grounds is taken that the Trial Chamber will necessarily admit an expert as such. And in the period immediately preceding the appearance of any expert, the Trial Chamber will be giving consideration, broad consideration, to the admissibility of the evidence in general. I imagine if the parties are not at issue over it that it will be influenced by that to a very large extent, but there will nevertheless be a decision to be taken by the Chamber about admission. But there are some of these -- the other -- the five to whom objection is taken that we would like to address this morning. And the first of these is the Witness Ingeborg Joachim. Now, Mr. Hannis, is that a matter for you or someone else in the team to be dealing with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Moeller will be addressing the issue regarding experts this morning, so I'm going to change seats with her because I think she can see you all better from here than from where she's presently seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Moeller, the Trial Chamber is having difficulty identifying the expert nature of this evidence. What is the actual evidence that is to be given that you say is of an expert nature?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we submit that there are three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the microphone on?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's on, yes. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That there are actually three aspects this expert can testify on. The first aspect which is, I think, is rather obvious from the report is victim impact. The witness testifies about particular impact the crime of rape has on victims, and we submit that this kind of witness has regularly testified in trials before this Tribunal. And in case it does come to a conviction on this crime, we think it is relevant. The second aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's take that one, first of all. You say you need to tell me how serious rape is, do you? You need a witness to tell me how serious rape is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, it's not about the seriousity of the particular crime; it's more the particular impact this particular crime in the context of the society in Kosovo has, not only on the victim herself but on the social community she's living in, on her family, and we submit that it's a specific situation due to the particular culture in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say, therefore, that if a rape doesn't have that sort of impact it makes it less serious? Is that your argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, that is not our argument, Your Honour. We just -- as this Tribunal hasn't heard, apart from the Milosevic case that was interrupted, any case on Kosovo from the Kosovo side as victims. We thought it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber to get some background about the particular cultural context, societal context these particular victims are living in, because it is different to other victims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and other parts of Kosovo, due to the Kosovar culture. That's why we think it could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you show me the part of the report that deals with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you give me a minute. It is the latter part of the -- of the report -- excuse me. It starts with an introduction into the general impact of rape as a crime, and it gives a little history of the society, the Medica Mondiale, the expert testifies for, and on part 4.2 it deals with Kosovo traditions of family life, gender roles, roots and sanctions, the traditional cultural view in Kosovo on rape. And this is the part I referred to regarding the first relevant aspect. It's page 24 and the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what are this witness's particular qualifications to deal with that aspect of culture in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This witness has been working in the Djakovica office of Medica Mondiale from 1998 onwards and has had direct dealings with traumatised rape victims in this area, so she has direct experience in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See, I will be surprised - I may yet be this morning - if any counsel for the Defence stands up and says rape in Kosovo is not serious. You actually are submitting that this Court would be incapable without expert guidance of adequately reflecting the gravity of rape on a widespread basis, if that is proved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I tried to say before, we think that the particular cultural aspects that apply to the Kosovo society are outside the general knowledge; and for this reason, this expertise may assist the Court in getting some insight into that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that make it more serious? That's what I want to know. I mean, the only relevance can be to sentencing on this particular point. Is it more serious because of that or what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It may be considered more serious if the impact, the overall impact, is not only concerning the witness, but also very strongly the family and the society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's the second aspect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The second aspect, Your Honour, is specifically relating to our rape victims/witnesses, and I would like to give you a concrete example. However, to do so I would ask you to go into private session for a very short while, because this witness I would like to refer to has testified in closed session before and we will apply to have her testify in closed session in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the witness referred to in the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. She is not referred to in the report, but her situation illustrates why the report may be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will generally be very reluctant to go into private session, except obviously for the situation you've just highlighted; that's a clear example when we would. But I don't see why we need to for the purpose of illustration in these circumstances. Try and illustrate it in general terms without reference to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I will not refer to her pseudonym then. This is a witness who gave two statements to the Tribunal. The first statement she gave in 1999, and the second statement she gave in 2002, so three years later. Now, in the first statement she did not mention that she was a rape victim. She testified about the incident in great detail, but she never mentioned that in the course of this incident she was also raped. Now, in 2002 she gave another statement and then she gave a very detailed account about what happened to her, namely that she was gang-raped several times during this incident. Now, in a trial where she testified formerly, the Milosevic trial, this witness was cross-examined savagely on the fact that she never mentioned the rape in her first statement. And we submit that the report of the expert Joachim also refers to the particular difficulty for women in Kosovo to actually tell their stories and to find the inner strength to come out to that, because on top of the particular problems that are related with these crimes, there is the societal context that often enough these women can't even have their family or their husband know about what happened to them because then they would be sent away from their families. And we submit that in this regard also the expert report is helpful and may help the Chamber to assess the reliability of the testimony of such witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you direct me to a particular passage that deals with that issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is page 39 of the report, point 6.5, and it is titled: Reasons for the survivors' difficulties to talk about being raped. It deals with the particular shame and the fear of consequences and aspects like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the third aspect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The third aspect is that, as Your Honour may have seen from our 65 ter witness list, we have about nine witnesses who testified -- who will testify about rape crimes. And in the indictment we charge rape as part of the persecution in the context of a widespread and systematic attack. And we think that the report also may serve, to a limited extent, in showing from the experience of the Medica Mondiale Association, and in particular the Djakovica office, that the -- the fact that we call less witnesses on rape does not mean that these were only single events that happened. And the report -- the expert refers to a number of -- of victims that were treated in the centre and about surveys undertaken by the centre that demonstrate that these crimes occurred on a wide basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the examples that are referred to in this report, are they confined to Djakovica or do they cover other parts of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, they are confined to Djakovica because this is where the office of Medica Mondiale is stationed. And we ask the witness to confine her statement to her direct knowledge, the facts she directly experienced herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do any of the nine witnesses who will give evidence -- or were any of them raped in the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would need to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the difficulties about this aspect that you may wish to address is that the report suggests that the objective of Medica Mondiale is to support these women, to give them help. It would be contrary to the ethos of the organisation, I think, to challenge the accusation of rape. And what you would be inviting the Tribunal to do on the basis of that evidence would be accept that, I think, in one example there were 45 rapes suggested in a period in Djakovica, you would be asking us to accept that. Now, if an investigating magistrate had investigated 45 cases of rape and presented a report in which it was plain that the allegations had been challenged, then that would be one thing and a situation where you might see hearsay evidence being admitted, but where the objective of the person compiling the report is to encourage complaints of rape, then you have to ask how this evidence could be adequately challenged by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we take that point. And as I, I think, said, it is a limited weight we would attach, ourselves, to this part of the report clearly. We do not ask the Trial Chamber to make findings on a certain number of rapes that occurred on the basis of this report. It may at some -- to some degree, however, I think bolster the evidence of live witnesses who experienced rape and in different municipalities. But we are not asking that to be evaluated as direct evidence of rapes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was certainly unable to find any witness listed who had been raped allegedly in Djakovica, but perhaps your new list that came in has a different witness who may fall into that category. But I would find it difficult -- speaking for myself, I find it difficult to reach a conclusion about the widespread nature of rape in Djakovica without an eye-witness -- any eye-witness at all coming to speak to having been raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We take this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there one of the Defence counsel who would like to take the lead on this issue? I mean, Mr. Zecevic, you have obviously priority, but it may be one of the others is more in a better position to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can speak about this. I can give you my own opinion. In actual fact, it is the position of this Defence - and I assume of the other Defence teams, too - that it is truly unacceptable to call this witness as an expert witness. In actual fact, no one is challenging the fact that rape is a serious crime. Rape is a serious crime anywhere in the world, from the most developed countries in the world to traditional societies. The consequences of that crime are substantially identical anywhere on this planet. At any rate, the crime of rape basically affects the victim, her family, and her immediate surroundings. In that respect, the situation in Kosovo is no different from the situation anywhere else. Also, in relation to the other argument, in relation to the other argument presented by my learned friend, the problem that appears in literature -- well, there is a great deal of literature about this. The problem of rape victims in general to speak about rape, to report it, and so on and so forth, so this truly does not only pertain or specifically pertain to Kosovo, as compared to any other place where such a crime would occur. It is a fact that in our view the witness does not have sufficient expertise for this type of expert testimony, at least the way it's been explained. In our view, it would be more reminiscent of a factual witness actually if she was involved in that situation in Djakovica. She could not really be an expert witness, because her knowledge on the basis of what she did in Djakovica does not provide sufficient argumentation for her ability to appear as an expert before this Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a question to raise that concerns me in this situation as far as Kosovo is concerned. I support this assertion and I presented that in writing. There is no difference between rape in Kosovo and Bosnia and so on and so forth, religiously and so on and so forth. But what is Kosovar? What does that actually mean? Kosovo is a geographical term. Kosovo is the term in Albanian, and Serbs say Kosovo and Metohija. Albanians, Roma, not to call them gypsies, and Albanians and Serbs. I'm putting my own ethnic group at the very end. They all live there. When you say that there is a Kosovar sensitivity, are you referring to the entire population of Kosovo or only Albanian women? If you are claiming that it is only Albanian women who are sensitive to rape, I will never agree with that, because that community has been in existence for hundreds of years. What happened happened. But they all live there. Are you going to present a racial or religious theory to me that women of a particular faith find it more difficult to be raped than others? This is a big issue that this expert can lead us to if you put the question that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, that is a misrepresentation, with all due respect, of what has been said. The submission was that -- the submission was that are cultural impacts in the community from which the women who will personally give evidence in this case come and that the attitude of their families can be quite distinct from the attitude of families from a different culture. It was not presented as a religious -- a purely religious issue. However, the question that you raise I am happy to put in its proper form to Ms. Moeller, which is: Are you submitting that this is a phenomenon that applies to Albanian families, in other words confining your submission to them, or is it broader than that in relation to Kosovo as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are confining this to the Kosovo Albanian women because of the specific traditions in the Kosovo Albanian community and the particular role females play in the Kosovo Albanian families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that answer the question, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just expressed my concern, you see. When you are using a geographical term and when there are several different peoples living there and there are different cultures -- but so I didn't understand. At least now I understand. Of course I disagree. But at least I understand now. It's important to understand. In the previous cases tried here, Omarska, and so on and so forth, I heard the same thing, that it is particularly difficult for Muslim women from Bosnia and Herzegovina as opposed to other women, but such experts were not called. Also, differences in terms of statements. All of us are very experienced and we have heard thousands of witnesses change their statements, but it is up to the Court to say whether the witness is telling the truth the first time or the second time. And the third thing that affects me the most, and that is why I asked this to be placed on the agenda -- rather, the Defence team. And that is the evaluation of hearsay evidence. I have the impression that the Prosecution has been resorting to this throughout. They are going to bring in someone from Djakovica now and say that this person talked to some unknown people and heard such and such a thing. Bring these people, call these people, call an expert who is going to say that your indictment is right and then we won't waste any time and then get another witness for sentencing purposes. Maybe you have an expert of that type, too, and then fine. I am about to retire, so I guess you're going to make me retire earlier, so you'll just be doing me a favour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I have to acknowledge, I'm not unused to histrionics in court, but, Mr. Fila, I do think the Prosecution's submissions deserve treatment with a little more respect than that particular submission has been treated this morning. I appreciate that you have serious points to make on this, but some of these, I think -- some of your submissions were based on, I think, a disingenuous misunderstanding of the Prosecution's submission. I would not like this trial to start off on a footing of incongeniality among the parties involved. If there is due cause for concern about the behaviour of any counsel, then I will be happy to address that should it arise, but I think that that was a rather excessive reaction to the submission made. While there is a great deal of substance in much of what you say, please don't devalue it by the histrionics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise immediately to my colleagues. I have known them for a long time, and I have a great deal of respect for them. I apologise to you also. I just wanted to speak in this jocular fashion. Perhaps it went a bit too far. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are there any other submissions to be made on this point? Mr. Bakrac, you were halfway to your feet before Mr. Fila started. Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wish to say something about the other aspect that the Prosecution referred to in connection with this witness, and my learned friend Mr. Fila raised this issue, in part. What concerned me was the following. If I understood my learned friends of the Prosecution correctly, the expert should, with regard to the second aspect, explain the differences in witness statements. I think that this is a key issue as far as the Defence is concerned. So if at an expert general level someone were to claim that in view of the milieu in Kosovo rape is not easily reported, then if not all -- in all cases, then in a majority cases we would have to have subsequent reporting. It seems to me that in the material that we have in the Prosecution the situation is the exact reverse. Many reports came in straight away. We see that this expert witness was in Djakovica. And in very few cases were the incidents reported only subsequently. So if it's that kind of a community, if it's that kind of general climate as far as rape is concerned, then the situation would have to be reversed. So indeed the expert witness cannot explain to us a very, very important issue, and that is the differences involved in these statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any other submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber are agreed that certainly in relation to the second issue raised by Ms. Moeller it would be appropriate for expert evidence to be led. The issue of victim impact is probably also one on which it would be appropriate for evidence to be led, but we are at one in telling the Prosecution that it seems to this Trial Chamber unnecessary to lead that sort of evidence, that no one on the Defence side has - as I expected - suggested that rape in any community, be it in Kosovo or anywhere else, is a very serious offence. Where this is much less certainty in the minds of the Trial Chamber is in relation to the third issue, because there is the possibility there of the introduction by the backdoor of hearsay evidence from people with no remit to challenge that evidence and then a submission following upon it of widespread rape in an area in circumstances where there is no direct evidence at all before the Chamber of rape in that area. Now, I suppose that's an issue that can only be finally determined once we get to the point of looking at the witnesses' evidence in the light of what's gone before in the trial. So what we can do today is simply indicate to the Prosecution that on the face of it the Trial Chamber finds substance in at least part of this report. We find that the witness is suitably qualified, through experience and also through her professional training, to give expert evidence. But the extent to which this report will be admitted and she will be allowed to give evidence will be determined in the period immediately before she gives evidence. Now, this may be a suitable opportunity to outline a process to be followed in dealing with experts. As I indicated earlier, in relation to each expert that the Trial Chamber will want to have a look at the report and the evidence that's intended to be led from the witness some time in advance of that witness appearing. So it would, I think, be appropriate for the Prosecution to raise it as an issue ten days or so or perhaps -- sufficient number of days before the witness comes to the Tribunal, I think, for you to change the arrangements if necessary, to raise the question of the extent to which the evidence will be admitted. It will be obvious to us from your witness lists roughly when the witness is proposed, but it will be for you to identify it more particularly as the witness is about to give evidence. Now, the other expert issue is the -- well, there are two in fact. There is a submission from a number of Defence counsel that -- in relation to the witness Phillip Coo. There is a submission that it is inappropriate to admit his evidence because he is and has been for some time an investigator, or at least an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor. There is some -- I think maybe one case in which this issue has been addressed in the Tribunal before, and we would welcome some guidance on whether that is a factor of significance in excluding a person as an expert. Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Indeed this very issue of employees of the Prosecution office testifying as experts in court has been addressed by several Trial Chambers already. In the Galic decision regarding experts Ewa Tabeau and Richard Philipps, it's a decision from 3 July 2002. The Trial Chamber held that the pure fact that these experts are employed by one of the parties does not exclude them as testifying as experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but when you say "employed," were they actually employees of the Office of the Prosecutor or were they simply engaged to carry out certain research and produce a report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, they were employees of the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- working in the Office of the Prosecutor. Then there is another decision in the Brdjanin case on another military expert named Ewan Brown. It's a decision dated 3 June 2003. And the Trial Chamber there held that the question that an expert is employed by one of the parties or paid by one of the parties is a matter of weight, if at all, but not of admissibility of an expert report. Further on, in the Milosevic case, as we submitted in our submissions on Mr. Coo dated 28 June 2006, in paragraphs 3 and 20, Mr. Coo testified already as expert in the Milosevic trial and the very same regards and concerns were raised by the amici in this trial. A hearing was held on this matter with the Trial Chamber on 9 September 2002, and, if you like the transcript pages, it's starting at 9946. And this discussion -- in particular the fact that Mr. Coo was already an employee in the Office of the Prosecutor for several years working on Kosovo-related matters was discussed, and the Trial Chamber there accepted the Prosecution's arguments that, if at all, this would be a matter that goes to the weight of the evidence but it should not exclude admission of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the Galic decision an appeal decision or a Trial Chamber decision?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, it's a Trial Chamber decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The matter didn't arise on appeal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the matter not arise on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed the Defence in Galic requested certification for appeal, but it was denied by the Trial Chamber in the Galic case at that time. So this matter has not yet risen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am of the view that the touchstone will be whether the expert witness could be suborned and if the expert witness, while he is within the employment of the Prosecution, could be suborned into writing a report, or into this -- then of course it has no weight, and it has a prejudice, a bias. But in case we can disassociate the two factors, one is the employment, and the other is the report that we have seen elsewhere, then that may be helpful. Could you kindly dilate on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, Mr. Coo has different functions in the Office of the Prosecutor. He is the head of the military analysis section, and as in this regard the superior of all military analysts in the OTP. At the same time, he is serving as expert on particular matters. And in this regard, I think it is relevant to underline again that Mr. Coo has also served as an expert in the Limaj trial, which was a trial against KLA accused, which dealt with the other side of the Kosovo conflict. So he clearly is specialised in the area of Kosovo and in military aspects relating to the particular conflict in 1998, 1999. But he is independent in that he gives his specific expertise in different cases and regarding different parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which Defence counsel would wish to address this issue? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, just a few questions that I'd like to raise in this regard. The Sainovic Defence team wrote about this on the 5th of October, 2005, and we dealt with a great many of these issues. I would just like to refer to what the Prosecutor said now and a few things that they wrote about earlier. What are the problems with Coo? Coo is someone who is employed in the OTP. He is directly interested in having the Prosecution case come through. Therefore, on the basis of that fact, he loses every necessary degree of impartiality and objectivity. He is an interested party here, and as such he cannot assess persons and events, as an expert should. In addition to that, Coo has another role here. Coo took active part in different stages of these proceedings, not only someone who wrote a report, the first, second, third, whatever version, but somebody who also took part in the generation of the evidence that is being presented. That is what makes this situation different from others. So we're not only saying that someone appeared as an officer of the Prosecution. He conducted numerous interviews with witnesses, suspects, potential witnesses. He took active part in this with his questions, positions. He affected the course of these statements. He affected what documents would be presented, also what knowledge and facts would be reached in these interviews. Through this activity, he overcame the role of an expert. He took active part in the creation of evidence. In some stage of these proceedings, perhaps he will have to appear as a fact witness to, for example, what one of the accused said to him, what one of the witnesses said to him, and so on and so forth. How does one reconcile then his role of expert and his predictable role of witness? What happens if an accused person says that he did not give him a certain document? This is hypothetical. But what happens if he says that he gave a false document? How are we going to resolve that if the man appears here in potentially two different roles that are mutually antagonistic? Your Honours, that is the reason why -- well, I don't want to dwell on it any longer. I don't want to use up more time, and I don't want to mention once again all the reasons that we've already presented. That is why this man should not appear here as an expert or a potential witness. Now, the OTP, I think, can opt for one of those two roles. By no means can one allow the situation, whereas -- whereby he would appear in both roles, and this is quite possible under the circumstances. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Petrovic, if you've any idea how many of the witnesses who will appear here he was involved with?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the number is quite substantial. I can't tell you now. I can tell you on Monday. But I can tell you in relation to the accused. At least two of the accused were involved -- he was involved in their statements. This went on for days, and he affected the very course of these statements by his own role. As for the number of witnesses, I don't have this at my finger-tips but I'm sure I can obtain this information very quickly. The information is available. I believe my learned friends know. There is more than one such witness. There is probably more than five, but I do not wish to speculate, and I ask to be given a chance to provide this information in one of our future hearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, every Prosecution witness is an interested witness. Again, the touchstone will be: Why is he antagonist in prosecuting the persons accused here? If you would kindly dilate on that, the matter will be absolutely clear, because if somebody is interested, all right, but then somebody has a reason to prosecute somebody with an antagonism and animus which he develops for him, well, then the value of the evidence has to be just nothing. Could you kindly tell us on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not believe that we can talk about antagonism here. I'm talking about his professional ambition for his team, a team which he's part of, to succeed in whatever they're doing, which leads to bias on his part. He wants to be successful, which is only natural. He was a military investigator and now he's a member of an investigating team. As someone who's an OTP employee, he wants to succeed. He wants to be the boss of an investigating team. As a neutral expert to appear before this Court, he should be rid of that sort of ambition. He is supposed to help you reach certain conclusions, and there should be no bias involved. At least that's my understanding of the situation. I don't think it is possible anywhere in the world to have evidence relating to that sort of expert analysis presented in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any other submissions for the Defence? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully agree with what my learned friend, Mr. Petrovic, has said. I would like to provide another example of this. There was a trial at this Tribunal where there was an expert report being used by a military expert who was also a member of the OTP. And there was a document that was an exculpatory document that was simply brushed aside and not analysed in that particular report. At a later stage, it became obvious that the Prosecution had been in the possession of this document all along, and a debate followed. The expert, when prompted, told us this briefly. When deciding whether to use this document in his report, in the OTP, within their own system at some level, there was a meeting at which a trial attorney decided simply whether this document should or should not be used. It was obvious in this case that although the expert had knowledge of this document, he received orders directly from one of the trial attorneys on the use of this document. I just wish to give you this as an example to show how dependent these experts are by their superiors within the OTP who, as we know, are an interested party and wish to succeed in their case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I think Mr. Aleksic wants to say something also, Mr. Hannis, unless -- or do you want to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to make a particular point about Mr. Visnjic's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we not deal with them altogether? I'm going to give you an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just had a particular concern about the nature of that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that it went to unnamed lawyers and an unnamed expert in our office. It has nothing to do with Mr. Coo or any lawyers on this team as far as I'm concerned, and I'm bothered by that. I just wanted to express that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think you can take it that we're alert to that weakness of it. But you'll have an opportunity to respond in due course to all these matters. Mr. Visnjic, do you want to say any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to confirm what Mr. Hannis just said. I do not have that team in mind. If necessary, however, I can forward to the Trial Chamber transcripts from the relevant case and then you can see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How quickly can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a day. I can give them to you on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not today?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with what my learned friends Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Petrovic have said. I would just like to add one thing in relation to OTP witness General Vasiljevic. He was interviewed. We have 18 CDs with his interview, about 60 hours. At least half f that time Mr. Coo was there while General Vasiljevic was interviewed. I just wanted to say that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would just like to wrap up and clarify a few points, particularly in light of the comments made by Judge Chowhan. I believe that, if, as I understood Ms. Moeller, she was trying to indicate that the role that Mr. Coo plays in the -- during his employment in the OTP is different from the subject matter of his proffered testimony, but I submit that if he is employed on a permanent or near-permanent basis as the head of the military analysis office of the Office of the Prosecutor, and if he is being proffered as a military analyst expert in this case, I submit he has a very strong incentive, if not biased, financial or otherwise, to keep his employment by tendering views that are favourable with the OTP's theory of the case and the allegations that they have in the indictment. And indeed I submit it would seem illogical for someone who were to express views contrary to the OTP's theory of the case to remain employed on a near-permanent basis in that office on that same topic. On another point -- so if that is what Ms. Moeller, my learned colleague, was implying, that he doesn't have that bias, I submit that he does, and it is a very serious bias. Secondly, the Prosecution offered other cases where -- where OTP employees have been accepted as qualified witnesses, but I submit one has to look at whether the witness has prior significant experience in the area that he is testifying in or being proffered to testify in. The witnesses mentioned, for instance, Tabeau, who is a demographer, had significant prior experience doing demographic work. I do not believe that Mr. Coo, based upon the information that has been provided to us, has had any significant prior experience, that is prior to coming to the OTP, in terms of studying or analysing the Serbian Ministry of the Internal Affairs, for instance, or the army of Yugoslavia, or the various structures within Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia upon which he is proffering his testimony. So I would submit it appears in Mr. Coo's case his expertise only arises through his role as an OTP employee and is directly linked to that position, and therefore we would strongly object to his use as an expert witness on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, I think on this occasion we do need to hear some more, particularly about the various things that have been said about the role played by Mr. Coo in investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. As we stated in our written submissions, it is correct that Mr. Coo assisted in interviews with suspects, witnesses, and some of the accused. It is important to know that of course he did assist the investigator or the lawyer or both of them at the same time with the interview. It was not Mr. Coo himself interviewing the witness on his own account. That's just as a clarification of the practice. Now, this practice is indeed a common practice in the Office of the Prosecutor that is done with regard to all military experts. In other cases this aspect has been raised as well, and just recently in the Mrksic trial I think Mr. Reynaud Theunens was asked in cross-examination also about his participation in witness and accused interviews. So far this particular point has never brought a Trial Chamber to exclude the report of a military expert. The Prosecution does of course not object to this issue being properly discussed with the witness in cross-examination, and Mr. Coo can, himself, best clarify, we think, in which interviews he took place -- he took part, excuse me, and which role he played therein. We again argue this is really a matter of weight to be attached to his report and then of admissibility, as the Defence appears to argue. Now, the other arguments raised by the Defence regarding his being dependent and therefore bias because he is employed by the Prosecutor's office. We think that lacks merit. We argue that because he is employed on a fixed-term basis by the Tribunal, he's actually more independent than an expert who would be hired on an ad hoc basically only. Mr. Phil is not paid -- he doesn't get a fee on the Prosecution's winning or losing a case. This plays no role in his work, and it has not played a role in any of the former performances he has done in other cases. And indeed in both in Milosevic and in Limaj his reports have been admitted, he was cross-examined, and all relevant aspects were discussed with him and upon that his report was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the fixed term?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Fixed term is an annual -- or one-year or two-year contracts, as I think all employees have here in the Tribunal. If I may add one argument regarding the allegation by the Defence that Mr. Coo influences -- or rather, that we influence Mr. Coo on his report and we order him to write the report in a certain matter; it's rather the other way around. Mr. Coo advises us, and we shape our case theory according to his advice. He is the expert, and he is the person who knows best the military and police aspects in this case, and of course there is no undue influence of any Trial Attorney or Senior Trial Attorney to make him write a report in a matter. We really reject this argument completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can I assist any further, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't addressed what might be the best point of all, that he is -- bearing in mind his background, the role he plays and his general self-respect, he will be professionally ambitious for his team to succeed. Is that not the best argument of all that's been advanced by the Defence, that he is part of a team and he's being proffered as an independent expert?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I -- as I thought I had addressed earlier, the military analysis section is a separate section within the Office of the Prosecutor. And Mr. Coo is not a member of this investigation team or a member of any other investigation team. He is assisting different teams within the Office of the Prosecution with particular matters relating to military and police structures, now specifically for Kosovo. As I raised, he assisted the Limaj team with regard to military and police aspects in the case against KLA accused, and he assisted in the Milosevic trial regarding aspects of the Serbian forces. And now he is assisting in the Milutinovic trial regarding these aspects. Likewise, other military analysts, like Ewan Brown, have assisted in various cases, including Brdjanin or Stakic; or Mr. Butler has assisted in Krstic. So officers of this section are assisting different teams, but I wouldn't consider them teams of investigation -- team members of investigation teams that are dependent on these investigation teams succeeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What was he doing before coming here, before joining you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Coo was an officer in the Canadian army, an intelligence officer, and we submitted in our written submissions on 28 June 2006, on page 2, paragraph 7 and the following some details on his training and his education. He received the generic training that military officers receive in the Canadian army, including training on command structures, et cetera. And he also actively participated in exercises and was member or corps member of a command structure at some point in his career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Besides him you have no other expert --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- of the same type. Do you have any other person as an alternate?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one other expert, Mr. De La Billiere, who is on the witness list, but he only talks about very generic matters regarding command structures, and Mr. Coo's report is of a totally different nature. If you look at the report, it contains hundreds of footnotes, and nearly each sentence in this report is footnoted with a document that was obtained either by request for assistance directly from Serbia and Montenegro, or by some of the accused who gave it to us, or by Defence witnesses who brought it forward in the Defence case of Mr. Milosevic's trial. And in this regard, his report is of a unique nature and we could not replace him with Mr. De La Billiere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the interviews that he has participated in have all been of military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Military or police personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that also include the interviews he participated in with the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe one additional aspect to point out is that he -- Mr. Coo in his report does not use any evidence obtained in these interviews, either of the accused or of other witnesses, to draw his conclusions or to base his theory upon. He only relies on documents that were gained in the way that I just described to you. There are no references of him to any of these interviews or statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: He was there to assist the interviewing Prosecutor or the interviewing investigator with his expertise because these command structures are very complex, and military documents, on the face of themselves, are not easily digestible. It's not general knowledge I think the ordinary lawyer or investigator would have, and he assisted on these particular aspects. We also think this is the strength of his report, that he may assist the Trial Chamber in understanding and finding an interpretation of the -- of the documents we will present at some point in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But his purpose at the interview is to give guidance to the investigator on how to conduct the interview, from what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No. He's not -- he's not giving guidance, but he is helping with particular aspects in regard to military issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give me an example then. I'm having difficulty understanding what it is, unless he's helping the investigator formulate questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, an example would be, for instance, that a VJ officer is interviewed, and Mr. Coo from his report and sources has the best knowledge of very minute details of which brigades may have been in which area at certain points, and he would assist with such details, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but assist in what way? Would he prompt the investigator to ask the right questions? I mean, what else is he doing there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, he himself did ask questions in interviews, too, on these particular aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're not seriously telling me the whole point of that is to go away and ignore what the answers were?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, of course not. Plenty, plenty of the Rule 68 evidence that we disclosed actually came from this participation of Mr. Coo in interviews and of him evaluating military and police documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I read your submission a moment ago as being that he only worked from documents which were recovered; he didn't use the results of any of the interviews. Now, I find it difficult to understand why the interview was taking place, if he wasn't going to make use of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, he was assisting us to get to the heart of the matter, and we may use this evidence then to call witnesses as fact witnesses. But he did not use the evidence he helped adducing in such interviews or statements as a basis of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, is the report like an ipse dixit, or is it having references to the research he may have made, original research he may have made. Ipse dixit would be a bare report on formulating a view on something he came across without substantiating it with the evidence available. So is it a report of that type or is it a report he's formulated on the basis of his research? Because the two are having different footings. Please can you say on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. His report is based, as I said, on a huge collection of documents that we will tender. He does -- he does set out the documents in the report, but he also offers an interpretation of the documents and puts them in context. Every offer of an interpretation, of a theory is grounded by a footnote referring to official documents of the army or the police, we submit. And Mr. Coo, at the same time while offering this interpretation, we think has been very careful not to touch upon the ultimate issue, which of course is for the Trial Chamber to determine. And he offers this expertise to the Trial Chamber to assist. And it is one interpretation, and certainly the Defence will, at some point, consider offering a different interpretation to these documents. But it is an argued report, footnoted and sourced and very detailed, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is an issue that the Trial Chamber can resolve, but we will not resolve it today. We will resolve it sometime in the course of next week, but I'm very grateful for these submissions. It will enable us to remove another contentious issue from the agenda early in the trial. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. You said you would be ruling on this next week. This might be a good time, bearing in mind that you will be ruling on this, to add something. I believe there's something that has not been entirely clarified. There was the issue of Mr. Coo's involvement for any assistance that he gave to the investigators while they were conducting the interview. I don't think this has been sufficiently clarified. Mr. Coo asked a number of questions himself to some of the accused and some of the witnesses, thereby directing the interview by asking questions to the accused himself, and quite a number of questions, if I may add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I don't find that a very persuasive argument because many experts have to carry out their own investigations, including interviewing people to prepare themselves for doing it. And it also has to be acknowledged that many experts are employed by government services or have, on the face of it, what might be arguably an interest in the outcome of proceedings. I think it's the particular circumstances of this case that we have to concentrate on, and that takes a little thought. That's why I can't -- we can't rule on it at the moment. We need to have a look at some of the report, I think, as well as the -- a further review of the CV of Mr. Coo and give consideration to the submissions made about how this sort of situation has been treated in other cases here. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to inform you, we have been successful in identifying the relevant portions in the transcript. After the break, I can give you the page numbers and the relevant paragraphs. You remember that problem that the OTP addressed and that I then discussed. We are finding this new technology extremely helpful after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll be grateful for that assistance. It's now time to interrupt -- sorry, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just quickly give you one more information. All these suspect interviews and the accused interviews are videotaped and recorded. So if the Trial Chamber has any doubts about Mr. Coo's direct participation and putting questions to witnesses, these tapes are available and it can be clearly seen what role he played in these tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll adjourn now for a half an hour -- or at least until 11.00. We'll try to resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to inform you that the transcript is from the Krstic case. The page is 9802 through 9804. An excerpt has been submitted by e-mail to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the third of these expert witness issues is the position of the constitutional expert Ivan Kristan and one particular issue relating to his potential evidence, and that is whether somehow or other he is barred from being presented as an expert because he played a role in some of the events about which he would give evidence. Now, do you have a submission to make on that, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would first like to refer Your Honours to our written submissions of 10 November 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where we dealt with Mr. Kristan in paragraphs 34 to 44. As to the history of Dr. Kristan, as you are aware of, he was also called as an expert in the Milosevic trial, and a hearing was held on the very same issue, whether his activity as a judge of the constitutional court at the time precluded him from being an expert on certain issues dealt with in his expert report. The Milosevic Trial Chamber on 23 May 2004, it's transcript pages 21161 to 62, held that due to a lack of disinterestedness in this expert, he could not testify as an expert on two aspects of his expert report; namely, the first two parts in the expert report relating to the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy and the right to self-determination and secession of the Republic of Kosovo. It's the parts in the expert report starting at page 7 and going to page 39 in the version we now also submit as the expert report. At the same time, the Trial Chamber in Milosevic did allow him to testify and did admit the other parts of his expert report, which related to issues not related to his former function of the constitutional court. There were parts relating to the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Serbia, and the FRY dealing with aspects relating there to federal law mainly. In our submissions in this case, we argue that the ruling of the Milosevic Trial Chamber to preclude him for the issues related to the autonomy of Kosovo and the right to secession are not binding on this Trial Chamber. As you know, only Appeals Chamber Judgements are binding for Trial Chambers, so the Trial Chamber would technically of course be free to adopt a different opinion on this issue. We would like to refer Your Honours again to the Brdjanin decision of 3 June 2003, which explicitly states that any matters relating to the independence and impartiality of the expert are matters of weight. We submit that on the basis of this jurisprudence the Trial Chamber could hear the expert also on the two matters that were not accepted by the Milosevic Trial Chamber and could take into account Mr. Kristan's former function as a judge of the constitutional court when attaching weight to his evidence. We also submit that his position as a judge on the constitutional court and the fact that he submitted an opinion on the very issue we ask him to submit an expert opinion in this court does not necessarily preclude him as an expert. It is correct that he did deal with the aspects concerned by his report in a separate opinion while being a judge on the constitutional court, but summarising this again, we think, if at all, that goes to really the weight attached and not to the admissibility of the report. To add to the history of Mr. Kristan in Milosevic, there is another ruling of the Milosevic Chamber dated 1st March 2005 called order on re-calling Dr. Kristan. And in this decision the Trial Chamber allowed Mr. -- Dr. Kristan to be re-called back as a fact witness in relation to the very two issues that he was not allowed to testify about as an expert. That occurred after the Defence in Milosevic had called a constitutional expert who was dealt with in a very detailed examinations. And the Trial Chamber in this order decided that Dr. Kristan would be called back as a fact witness testifying to the autonomy of Kosovo and the revocation of its autonomy and the right to self-determination. So we submit that in the alternative, should the Trial Chamber not accept Mr. Kristan as an expert on the two issues that relate to his previous position as a constitutional judge, then we would apply for Mr. -- for Dr. Kristan to be called as a fact witness on these matters. That would conclude my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Moeller. Now, who for the Defence would like to take the lead on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- [In English] Thank you very much, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In our submission on the 27th of August, 2004, we expressed our views in detail with regard to the expert, Professor Ivan Kristan, and Mr. Budimir Babovic. I would just like to make a few brief comments with regard to what my learned friend just said. It is a fact that Mr. Ivan Kristan was a court of the -- a judge of the constitutional court, and then on the basis of his participation in the debate before the constitutional court of the constitutional changes, rather, the amendments to the constitution of Serbia in 1990 -- well, on the basis of these facts, the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case concluded that there were not sufficient grounds -- or rather, that he was not an interested party [as interpreted]. So from that point of view, his expert opinion was rejected in that part. This is where the problem lies. As opposed to the Milosevic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was your submission he was not -- or was your submission that he was an interested party?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, he was an interested party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript. On you go, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I couldn't check the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that the Milosevic case consisted of three indictments, covering a period from 1990 -- or rather, 1992 up to 1999. Our indictment covers the period from 1999 -- well, with a certain part of 1998. At that time, what is relevant for this Trial Chamber and what the task of a constitutional expert would be is to explain the constitution of the socialist -- no, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Serbia and their mutual relationship. Mr. Kristan, in his explanation of this expertise, stated very explicitly that he did not deal with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. So those two constitutions that are of key importance and their mutual relationship, as far as this case is concerned, was not actually the subject of Mr. Ivan Kristan's professional interest. Mr. Ivan Kristan in his CV states that he wrote 24 papers, out of which ten were published before 1990 and, for the most part, pertained to the constitution of the federal republic -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the law on associated labour and so on and so forth and the relations among the federal republics within the former Yugoslavia. After that, after 1990, he published yet another 14 other papers, none of which remotely deal with the subject matter that is of interest for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I might interrupt you there, Mr. Zecevic. I don't think it's appropriate at this stage to go into a general challenge to the expertise of Dr. Kristan. The one issue that the Trial Chamber feel they might be able to resolve at this stage is the question whether his membership of the constitutional court, the factors that led the Milosevic Trial Chamber to exclude him as an expert on certain subjects, should be regarded as excluding him or preventing him from giving expert evidence in this trial. Now, you're identifying possibly a question of relevance, bearing in mind that this trial is about 1999. And that's a matter we might address I think in a different context nearer the time of hearing his evidence. Could you confine your submission, please, to the question whether the fact that he was involved in some of the events ought to preclude him from being viewed as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I most certainly agree with you, Your Honour. I turn to the question of relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you're agreeing with, but please don't consider me as having indicated a firm view on anything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said I agreed, my understanding was the Trial Chamber was expecting me to state my position -- or rather, the Defence team's position concerning this special situation or, rather, his position as a judge attached to the SFRY constitutional court. However, I took the opportunity to speak about relevance in general because that was the other thing that my learned friend had previously addressed. She offered another option for him to be heard as a factual witness and not an expert in relation to one portion of his evidence and as an expert in relation to another portion of his evidence. That's what I have to say about the relevance, but if the Trial Chamber wishes to hear this on a different occasion, we can leave that for later. As for the question just asked by the Chamber, we fully support the ruling in the Milosevic case. We did say that in our brief on the 27th of August, 2004. We believe that the fact that he was a member of the trial chamber of the SFRY constitutional court when this issue was ruled upon eliminates him as a potential expert witness on this issue, since we definitely believe that he would be interested in reinforcing his position after some time has elapsed and to corroborate his position by using the same arguments that he had already provided at the time. His expert report or his evidence as an expert will not achieve a level of quality that might help us or the Trial Chamber to approach the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's the difference between that situation and a situation where an academic expert gives evidence in one case and then gives the same evidence in a later case, particularly where his evidence has been accepted in the first case, why is that any different from the situation where, as a member of a court he expresses an opinion, as an impartial member, a man subject to all the controls and expectations that arise when you're a judge. Why should that level of impartiality displayed on a previous occasion disqualify him from expressing that opinion on a later occasion? I mean, I, for one, at the moment am entirely unpersuaded by the Milosevic decision, and that's why I raise this matter at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With the permission of the chair, I have a comment to make. As I understand the decision in that case regarding this witness was to an interlocutory order and it was not a judgement to play the position of a ratio decidendi. So it will not be a ratio decidendi. Even talking about it would be something said in obiter, and what was said in obiter is not binding at all, especially with us here or any other because it was obiter. It was never a ratio decidendi and it was just a -- because ultimately had they decided and given a view, that would have been different. So I would say that can't be quoted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just in case there is any misunderstanding here, it was in fact a decision because the witness did give evidence and was prevented from giving expert evidence on these two matters, but it was a decision by a Trial Chamber, which is not binding on this Trial Chamber, although it has to be respected in any determination we make. But the matter never got to the Appeals Chamber, and therefore there is no binding authority in this situation. Carry on -- if you can help me on that issue, Mr. Zecevic, which is one that has puzzled me since I saw the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree with the Trial Chamber and, above all, I fully with my learned friend who has provided essentially the same explanation as the Chamber. There was a decision in the Milosevic case which is in no way binding this Chamber. I do agree. The fact is, however, that the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case discussed this same situation and passed the decision that it did. There is no doubt about that. What we see as a potential problem for Mr. Kristan here is the fact that in the previous case he was not really an expert. He was one of the judges who ruled on an issue before the federal constitutional court. His opinion diverged from the majority opinion at the time. The majority adopted the final decision. That is another fact. His opinion, as such - and I fully agree with the Trial Chamber - is perfectly justified. Any judge is entitled to an opinion or to a dissenting opinion. The fact, however, remains that a decision was made; a decision was made by the federal constitutional court. At the time the decision became part of the legal system. If it is a majority decision, then it has full legal force, the constitutional court being the supreme legal institution in that country at the time. As far as that is concerned, Mr. Kristan or any other expert would have to quote that decision as being a part of the legal system of that country at the time. This decision was adopted in a perfectly legitimate procedure. In his expert report he defends his own dissenting opinion, which was not a majority opinion in that case.
