Bearing that in mind, I believe the Trial Chamber in the Milosevic case believed, as we believe, that his expert opinion could not be viewed separately from the context of this fact, and this fact is what it is, it is a fact. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I agree with that. And I also think that if the decision was made properly, then that's a fact that no one can do anything about. But that's -- so that's a rather different question which wasn't the basis for the Milosevic decision. The basis was the very fact that he had played any part at all in the events barred him. Anyway, I'm grateful for that submission. Is there any other counsel that wishes to supplement that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This might be a suitable opportunity to make a couple of comments about the matters forming the subject of the trial, in light of the broad submission that Mr. Zecevic made just now. There is a question mark in the minds of the Trial Chamber about the general relevance of Dr. Kristan's evidence, bearing in mind that much of it is about matters of law and comparison of constitutions on which the Trial Chamber considers itself equipped to deal with the matter without guidance. However, that matter may have to be reviewed in more detail nearer the time the witness gives evidence. We're also concerned about just how important events in 1988 to 1991 might be in the context of this indictment, and even more concerned about what relevance might be found in events around 1980 and shortly thereafter in relation to this indictment. And therefore, there are a number of issues yet to be determined prior to the time when Dr. Kristan is envisaged as a witness about his evidence in general. On this particular point, however, we will, I think, be able to make a determination, and we shall do so in the same decision as we issue in relation to the witness Coo, and that will be in the course of -- sometime in the course of next week. But bear in mind that the decision is confined to the particular point that was raised in the agenda. Now, that completes the matters relating to experts, except to confirm the general indication given in the agenda, on which I think everyone was agreed in any event, that whatever expert gives evidence will be available for cross-examination. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just add one piece of information regarding Dr. Kristan. At a Status Conference held shortly after Dr. Markovic testified in Milosevic, you, as a Pre-Trial Judge, already raised the issue of the relevance and whether this is evidence that should really be led in trial. And upon these orders by you, we started sending out letters to the Defence setting out all the laws and constitutions, and we sent them to the three original accused on 2nd May 2005 and to the other accused on 29th September 2005. At that time, in September 2005, we also supplied the Defence with all the laws and constitutions on a CD and asked them whether they could agree that these constitutions and laws, as such, existed. Unfortunately, we haven't heard back on that, and in the pre-trial briefs of the Defence, we just went through them again, they have not agreed on any of these laws or constitutions. So we have attempted to obtain an agreement on these laws and constitutions and in order to reduce the amount of time we would use to lead such evidence in trial. However, to no avail so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, this is a matter which I have a little later in the agenda. I was going to deal with it under the heading in the second section about the agreement on facts. But just give me a moment, would you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, let's address this issue just now. It -- I don't envisage that today we are going to make much progress on agreed facts, but this has been an area on which goodwill was expressed by the Defence towards trying to reach agreement with the Prosecution on what the law actually is. In other words, it's a pure issue of authenticity. It's nothing to do with the impact or effect of it, which is a matter of interpretation, but a question of what is the law at any given time relevant to the indictment. Now, if Ms. Moeller is right that there hasn't been any progress made towards resolving this, then it's a bit disappointing in view of the indications, at least, that were given earlier. Now, can someone assist me on that? Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what the situation is. As far as the Defence is concerned, I am speaking generally on behalf of all the Defence teams now, we absolutely stand by what was said at our previous conferences, where we stated that we absolutely have no problem with relevant laws and regulations that were in force at that time in the country and the text of these regulations, as published in the Official Gazette of the then-FRY or Republic of Serbia or Kosovo or any other socio-political unit. We have absolutely no problem with that. However, this is what the situation is. In the meantime, we got from the Prosecution an offer to agree on a great many facts. Then - how should I put this? - we responded to that, and these facts included these laws. Trying to resolve several matters in a minimum of time, we wanted to include all of this in a general agreement on facts, including stipulation as far as laws and regulations are concerned. However, the problem was that we did not get that document in a language understood by our clients and of course we have to get instructions from our clients with regard to facts. I'm not talking about laws now, because that's different, but that was part of that document. So we would have to get that in Serbian so that we could get instructions from our clients. At that moment we would be quite ready to reach an agreement on facts with the Prosecution, as we said in advance to the Trial Chamber that we are not going to challenge the facts that have to do with laws and regulations. In my opinion, it is really just a technical detail at this stage. It's not -- [In English] I see that Your Honour wants to pose a question, so that's why I stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I can understand why certain matters of fact require translation for discussion with the accused, but so far as what was the law at the time is concerned, why can't that be dealt with as a separate, discrete issue on the basis of what was submitted to you? Is there any reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is I believe -- of Your Honour's, the problem is that we got a separate submission that has to do with the law that has to do with the stipulation of legal norms that were in force at the time. After that, soon after that, we got a document that included agreement on facts, including the previous document regarding legal regulations and norms. That is why we thought that the subsequent document actually embodied the position of the Prosecutor. So we wanted to resolve this in that way. If the Trial Chamber is instructing us to deal with this separately, we are prepared to deal with it on Monday, or perhaps even today, time permitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to assist my colleague, Mr. Zecevic, and to remind you of the following. The last position by the Defence, I would like to remind you of that, was that we accept the text in the Serbian language, as they were published in the Official Gazettes, in the photocopies of the material that we got from the Prosecutor. As for the translations and the discussions on that, this turned into a problem because of the translations into English, but we did accept the documents that were submitted to us in the original language and we did not have any objections to that. What we are discussing now is perhaps an additional element in terms of whether we are going to conclude that material in the stipulations, as proposed by the Prosecution, 400 or so individual items. As far as the documents themselves are concerned - and my colleagues can correct me if I'm wrong - we accepted them as they stand in the original language. We did not go into the translations, and we have not analysed that until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave may I just add to what my colleagues have said, but I do subscribe to everything they said. The Serb versions of these documents, as published in the Official Gazettes, that is what we are ready to accept. However, we want to say that in that set of documents there are some documents that are actually not the texts of laws or by-laws or of the constitution. We are agreeing only to laws and by-laws that were published in appropriate Official Gazettes of appropriate socio-political entities, that is to say republican, provincial, and so on. That is our acceptance of it. However, as for legal and factual conclusions that could be drawn on the basis of this, we do not agree to that. That will remain for our own argumentation and your own ruling, Your Honours, ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is obvious. But, Mr. Petrovic and others, please bear in mind that regrettably - and I do greatly regret that I'm not fluent in every language that is relevant to the case - regrettably, it will not be of great assistance to the Judges if you agree the Serb text and refuse to agree the English translation. Now, we have to overcome that difficulty in some way, and it would be rather petty, I would suggest, if we're not able to work out a methodology for reaching agreement on the English text. Each of the three Judges dealing with this case will expect to review the documents in English. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- this is the list of the -- of the laws and constitutions we're talking about, and it's a rather tiny list. We would like to clarify. These are texts taken from the Official Gazettes of Serbia of the FRY, and these are all official texts. We disclosed them in B/C/S and in English, so from that time onwards they had these documents in both languages. And this argument does -- I think lacks really merit. In addition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- with respect, the indication being given by Mr. Visnjic is that the position for some time has been that the text in Serbian, so far as published in a gazette, is accepted by the parties. Now, we're at least over the hurdle of agreement on what the law actually was, but for practical purposes, we need to go a stage further and we need to be able to agree on the English text. Now, how are we going to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the Defence could point out in relation to which documents they have concerns regarding the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was each of the translations done by CLSS here or are they unofficial OTP translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. The interpreters missed a certain section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the interpreters have missed the start of your submission there. Your microphone is on now, but you were leaning away from it. If you could start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Before me I have a list of documents that the Prosecution disclosed on the 29th of September, 2005. These are documents in the Serbian language, the photocopies of the excerpts from Official Gazettes, the documents that we referred to just a moment ago. On the right hand, in that column where there should be translations into English, I'm telling you now tentatively that, say, in about 70 cases, it says "translation requested." Only at one particular place does it say -- in one column it says "CLSS translation requested," which is what we would actually want. The other documents are, for the most part, untranslated, or some have draft translations, whereas some were seemingly taken over from the Milosevic case but with CLSS translations. So we are debating translations here now. Who translated the documents? And once we get these records -- well, of course I will stand corrected if I made a mistake in this, but we are prepared to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've had sufficient discussion to deal with this. At the resumption after the mid-day break, which will be -- we'll be resuming at probably -- I think it was programmed for 2.00, was it, the resumption? 2.00. Well, whatever that time is, it will be 2.00 or it may be a bit later, we'll make a decision about that at the time. After that break, I would like you to present to the Chamber a list of the laws published in the gazette that are accepted by the Defence from the list submitted by the Prosecution. Now, that gets over the hurdle of agreement on the law, the language being the Serbian language. That will also allow time for the Prosecution to identify which documents have been formally translated and intimated, and to draw that to the attention of the Defence, who seem to be in doubt that that has actually happened in relation to the bulk of these documents. And you should be able to tell us how far along the road you are to at least having in everyone's hands English copies. There may then be some time necessary to reach agreement that the translations are entirely accurate. So can we proceed that way? It's something that shouldn't take up more Bench time, I think, in the course of this hearing. All right. Thank you. Now, the next matter -- I'm sorry. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just a very short instruction from the -- well, we're seeking instruction from the Trial Chamber. There is a certain number of laws which were -- which were part of the legal system of Serbia and FRY at the time which are not in that list. We think these -- these laws are applicable and would need to be presented one way or the other during the trial, either in the OTP case or the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please try to do the same with them. You should be submitting a list of additional ones that you think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may -- with all due respect, if I may -- if I may suggest something: That we keep this as an ongoing process. That we provide the document today, which we will make the agreement with the OTP, and in future, if we would have, we would then present some other agreements on the other laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of doubt, common sense is the fundamental law that applies in this trial. And anything of -- any suggestion of that nature will be welcomed by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That then takes us to the next listed item. We received this week a motion for protective measures, the seventh motion submitted by the Prosecution. Now, I suppose normally this would go through a bureaucratic process of written responses, but it did seem to the Trial Chamber that it may be possible to cut through that in relation to this particular motion because we've dealt with the others by agreement in a particular way. Now, in this case does any Defence counsel take exception to the motion and invite the Trial Chamber to do something different from what it's done in relation to the other motions for protective measures? The absence of response suggests no to me. The one difficulty that we have to overcome immediately, however, is that at least two of the three witnesses referred to are not on the 65 ter list that I had prior to today, and that needs to be resolved -- in fact, it may be that the first thing to do, Mr. Hannis, is address the 65 ter list that's presented today and to tell us if these are the only two additions or if there are any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, they aren't the only two additions. And if I may, I'd like to go briefly through all the changes between the list that was filed in May and the list that we filed yesterday. We have five new witnesses to the list. Those include the witnesses K78 and K79 for whom we've requested protective measures in that seventh motion, a witness named Branimir Aleksandric, a witness Mahmut Halimi and witness Bislim Zyrapi. I think on the list -- if you have the list in front of Your Honours, these are numbers 163 through 167. We put them on at the end of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, have the statements for the ones for whom you don't seek protective measures been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They have, Your Honour, with regard to the last witness Bislim Zyrapi. An earlier statement of his disclosed, a supplemental statement of his was in the process of being taken yesterday, and we expect it will be completed and finalised early next week and disclosed, I think we said by the 14th of July. And with regard to the protected witnesses, Your Honour, at this point we've only disclosed redacted statements in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's deal with this first of all. Is there any objection from any Defence counsel to the addition of any of the five witnesses to the list? All right. No objection to that. So the Trial Chamber will allow the addition of these witnesses to the witness list. The second question, and I think it's already been answered, but just in case there's any doubt on it, does any Defence counsel take any exception to treating the seventh motion in the same way as earlier motions for protective measures and granting them in the way that we've granted the others? No one takes exception to that. So the motion will be granted in similar terms. But you have raised another issue, I think, in your proposed agenda, Mr. Hannis, which is to alter decisions made earlier, in light of the possibility of one or more of the accused not returning from provisional release after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. There are a number of witnesses for whom we had requested delayed disclosure. The Trial Chamber had ordered that that disclosure be made on the 31st of July. The 31st of July now also happens to be the date upon which all the accused are to return after the provisional release that will be granted to them for two weeks during our recess. Part of our -- part of our argument previously regarding that date for delayed disclosure had related to our suggestion to the Court that we had mentioned some witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I cut through this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's no -- it's no accident that these dates are, I think, now the same. Perhaps it would have been more convenient if one was earlier than the other slightly, but the fact of the matter is I think they have to return by a certain time on the 31st of July.

utterances.text: Thank you. So that, I think, deals with the seventh motion for protective measures and associated witness issues, that's the 65 ter list.

utterances.text: It's probably convenient to deal with them as well. We just want to know that everything that needs to be done has been done.

With regard to Braddock Scott, we have an ICTY statement which we have disclosed. We are still in negotiations trying to do that. I know Friday -- yesterday was my deadline, Your Honour, and I am reporting to you on the status of that and our ongoing efforts to obtain statements to disclose in relation to those last two. And I should say, we had at one time told Your Honour we thought there would be possibly as many as six US Rule 70 witnesses. We are now intending only to call four, those four I just named.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's only right that I should give you some notice, Mr. Hannis, that in relation to Wesley Clark, I will certainly require some persuading that he should be treated the way he was treated in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I have not reached any final agreement or instruction from the provider in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there is a controversial issue there. I don't know anything about the other three -- at least I don't know sufficient about the other three to make any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think there would be anything of the same level of requirements. And with regard to Mr. Clark, I think the circumstances have changed that I hope won't make those not so important this time [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis, for that comprehensive explanation of the up-to-date witness situation. Does any Defence counsel have any comment to make about the various things that have been said about changes in witness arrangements? All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly. I have spoken to some of my learned friends, by no means all. I hope that I'm expressing a joint position, despite this. As soon as we receive written motions on these circumstances, changes in the witness status and so on and so forth, we would like to reserve the right to put forward our position then. That is what I have to say at this point in time about these changes proposed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite understand what you're saying. I mean, I understand that if you're -- I understand what you're saying if it's confined to the four American Rule 70 witnesses, but if you're saying something about -- that goes beyond that, I don't follow the point you're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we heard that some witnesses, for example, those who have died, will be submitted as 92 bis (C) witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I understand that. Yes, exactly. These ones plus the Rule 70 witnesses; I follow what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just again a general comment that I know that it's pretty standard practice here for motions in any circumstances to be made in writing, and often that's encouraged, depending on circumstances; however, the Bench can often be greatly assisted by oral discussion of matters. And we, in principle, will have no objection to oral motions being made, but we would not want them made without notice. So if you wish to present a motion orally, then that will be perfectly acceptable as long as adequate notice is given for your opponent to prepare to respond. But please bear in mind also that the court time is most valuably used in hearing evidence, and therefore I would ask you to do that with discretion. It's even possible, I suspect, to arrange hearings to consider motions, depending on the availability of courtroom space, that wouldn't interfere with the hearing of evidence. But listening to witnesses, causing them the maximum -- the minimum inconvenience will be the prime objective of the way in which the Court manages the use of court time. Now, the final matter in the section, in the first section, of this agenda is the request by Mr. Visnjic that his client should make a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis, following upon the Prosecutor's opening statement. And, as you know, the rule provides for such a statement being made under the control of the Trial Chamber and gives the Trial Chamber authority to decide in their discretion whether or not to permit this to happen. And notice was given to you, I think, Mr. Visnjic, that the Trial Chamber would like you to explain the purpose and nature of the statement that's proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. I thank you for giving me the opportunity to brief you on this. General Ojdanic wishes to make an 84 bis statement. As far as I know, and I do believe I know what he would like to say, he would like to introduce himself to the Trial Chamber and say a thing or two about his background. The next portion of his statement relates to the substance of the indictment and his own mens rea when these events took place. As far as I know - and I do believe I know sufficiently to say - General Ojdanic will be speaking about things related to the indictment and will not go any further than the framework of the indictment itself or its legal implications. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That allows him awfully broad scope, Mr. Visnjic, in view of the way in which this indictment is framed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall try to use up probably not less than half an hour, but certainly no more than an hour. May I add something, Your Honour? General Ojdanic was first indicted seven years ago. He has not spoken publicly about the indictment so far, especially as regards any of the detail of the indictment. He has not had many opportunities to address this publicly. I think this is an opportunity for him to express the strong feeling that he has that he stands indicted yet he is innocent. I do not think there will be anything in his statement that would go outside the scope of the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ojdanic, could you just stand, please. Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you can perhaps clarify for me the basis on which the accused -- I haven't paid any attention this morning to the position of the accused until now. What's the basis on which they've been invited into the dock? I thought there would be some logic to the order in which they sat in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why the accused are not sitting in the order in which they appear in the indictment? That's my simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I can explain. I think as they entered the courtroom this morning they just sat down. I think that is the only rational explanation that I could possibly offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So, Mr. Ojdanic, you are to be permitted by the Trial Chamber to make your own opening statement, following upon the opening statement of the Prosecutor. Mr. Visnjic has given a clear indication that the statement will be confined to an introduction of yourself, an explanation of your background, and comments you wish to make about the substance of the indictment and your own mens rea, your own mental state and understanding of things, at the time of the events in the indictment, and that what you say will not extend beyond matters raised in the indictment. The Trial Chamber will monitor carefully the statement you make, because these statements are designed to assist the Trial Chamber to reach a determination of issues raised in the indictment. I'm particularly concerned that in this trial the issues that are addressed by the parties are entirely forensic issues and that we do not extend into the political arena, beyond the extent to which that is absolutely necessary. So I ask you to bear carefully in mind these remarks when deciding exactly what you will say in your opening statement. Thank you very much. You can be seated again. THE ACCUSED OJDANIC: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to live up to that expectation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I see that we've already dealt, to some extent, with the next matter, which was agreement on facts. And we've made some progress in relation to issues of law, at least the fact of the law, as it were. There is a Prosecution document circulating seeking agreement on a very wide range of facts, some of which, Mr. Hannis, you must know in your heart of hearts, there wasn't the remotest prospect of any agreement being reached on. In relation to some you might as well have said: I plead guilty. Now, it's a bad starting point to have an agenda or a negotiating document which goes way beyond any realistic expectation. On the other hand, it's plain that there is material which is capable of agreement, and we've recently received an indication on behalf of General Ojdanic that there can be agreement on a number of issues. I haven't explored that in detail to see just exactly what it amounts to. And there's a limit to what we can do in the context of this hearing. So my question to you is: Do you see a way forward on this at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Your Honour, but I would report to you that we had also received from Mr. Ackerman an e-mail on the 2nd of June in which he agreed to a number of those 388 proposed agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I have to say, Mr. Hannis, that to agree that Kosovo is generally in the southern part of Serbia is a pretty pointless agreement. That's a notorious fact that the Trial Chamber would take account of anyway. I'm trying to address myself to productive agreement on fact. Now, do you see a way forward in any area by restricting this in some way and trying to discuss it further or is it a dead duck?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's certainly lame, if not dead. We have -- but -- and I take your point about some of these facts seem to be extremely basic, but it's been my experience that sometimes if you just get the ball started rolling and somebody can agree, yes, the lights are on in the room, then you can move to something a little controversial. That's part of our thinking in starting the way we did. Now, I realise we probably weren't going to get all the way to the end, as you mentioned, but I am generally an optimist and that was part of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there is a measure of agreement, and it may now be some matters which are agreed by everyone, I don't know, but do we have to compile now some sort of analysis of what has actually been offered by each party?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we do, as we said in one of the prior 65 ters, Your Honour. If five of them agree to a fact and the sixth one doesn't, it seems to me I probably need to present evidence to prove that fact. In addition to the particular responses of General Ojdanic and General Pavkovic's to those proposed agreed facts in the Defence pre-trial briefs, we did have some agreement to some things, but I do think we do have to come up with a master chart to track all those and see if there are anywhere we have all six agreeing to something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, some -- some analysis has been carried out by the Trial Chamber to try to identify any common ground in the various things said in the pre-trial briefs and the other documents that have been tendered indicating some basic agreement. When this job was done about ten days ago, there was nothing to which everyone had stipulated. It's now clear this morning that there are matters on which everyone will agree, in particular the -- what the law was at relevant times. There also have been some developments, including the submission received in the last 48 hours. So this analysis can be updated to reflect all that's been said by the parties so far. If it would be of assistance, what I would propose to do is circulate to you our understanding of what parties have offered to agree as the starting point, the ball -- the start of the snowball that Mr. Hannis hopes might roll into something more substantial. Now, does anyone say this is pointless? All right. Well, in that case, this document will be revised and will be circulated to you as our understanding at the moment of what's agreed or virtually agreed by parties. I suppose we should also reflect what even one or two parties have said they will agree to, since it might encourage others, I suppose, to go at least that far. But it would be in the context of expectation; in other words, we would be expecting you to seriously consider whether you can go that bit further, whether there are things, basic facts, that aren't notorious so that we're going to take judicial notice of them anyway, but basic facts that you can accept to avoid the leading of unnecessary evidence, particularly material that you know is not, in the end of the day, going to turn out to be controversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been drawn to my attention that there may even be matters on which there's been further discussion among you and potential agreement that we don't know about. And this would also form a trigger for you to alert us to anything of that nature. So it will be circulated with an accompanying order suggesting or proposing a date by which you should, as counsel for the Prosecution and the Defence, report on what has been possible, if anything, to agree on beyond the terms of the document. Now, that's a suitable point at which to adjourn. We will adjourn now until 2.15. We will resume at 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, that seems to take us to the question of whether and to what extent you might be contemplating making use of Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I address that, I did want to introduce another member of our legal team. Seated next to Ms. Moeller in the back is Patricia Fikirini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see her for the pillar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: She will be joining us this afternoon and you'll be seeing her during the trial, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, regarding 89(F), Your Honour, we have had a look through our witness list with that in mind. I would indicate to you that during next week's presentation, three of the witnesses that we are calling next week we intend to use 89(F), at least in part. And when I say that, Your Honour, it's our intention that we will have a written statement of the witness that we propose to submit under 89(F), but we will also be leading them in court, partly to expand on certain things in their statement or to make connections between paragraphs in the statement. The reason for that, Your Honour, is some of these 89 statements are basically their prior ICTY statement that was maybe made some time ago or was made specifically for the Milosevic case and doesn't pertain maybe as directly to our case as we would like, and not having had a chance to bring these people here and sit down and compose a complete new statement, we propose to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is exactly what the Trial Chamber envisaged you might do and hoped you would do and indeed hope that the Defence will do in due course. And this applies to the 92 bis witnesses as well. Because we've decided that all of them should be cross-examined, then it seems to me wrong that the witness should be simply sat down and cross-examined. But the bulk of the evidence is there in writing. It helps us to prepare properly for the hearing. It helps the Defence to prepare. It makes the cross-examination likely to be more focussed. But the witness has to be made to feel comfortable. It would be quite wrong to put a witness into the witness box and then subject that witness immediately to an aggressive cross-examination. The aggressive cross-examination may be necessary, but that witness should be given time to feel comfortable in court. So to me there is nothing at all inconsistent, and indeed I would encourage the use of these written statements in combination with oral evidence to the extent that the oral evidence is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm very happy to hear that, Your Honour. We're thinking along the same lines. We did look at our witness list, and as I'm speaking at the moment it appears that there are another 24 witnesses that we certainly intend to use Rule 89(F) with. I don't know if you want me to name those persons or give you a filing later on or indicate when we're submitting our weekly or monthly schedules that we intend to use 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I want is to devise a system now for dealing with this, because it seems to me that the Defence should have the material a reasonable time in advance of the witness giving evidence. Now, that's not always been the case in the past in trials here. A lot of material has been provided at very short notice in some instances, and the Bench would welcome the material. It may be the Defence need it earlier than the Bench. Desirable for me to have it the night before rather than earlier, because there's not much I can do with it getting it earlier, but the Defence may be able to do more productive work on it by getting it earlier. So do you have an idea of a sort of time-scale that you will generally try to operate? With reference to next week, for example, what do you see as being the time at which you're likely to give the Defence the 89(F) versions of the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, partly that depends on to what extent it contains new material. Your Honour, for example, Goran Stoparic is a witness scheduled for next week who we propose to proceed in part through Rule 89(F). He had given three prior statements to the OTP that relate to matters in addition to Kosovo, and so we've taken portions from each of those three statements that relate only to Kosovo and combined them into one new statement. So it really contains nothing new substantively, but it's just organised differently to focus primarily on Kosovo. We are getting that document ERN'd today and hope to furnish it to them at the end of the day, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. But I don't think you should rely too much on the idea that the material has already been available. It's been available in a different form, and it's going to greatly assist the progress of this case if the form in which its going to be used is the form that's given to the Defence at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I'm delighted to hear that. Now I hope you'll take the line that where you do have a statement well in advance of a witness giving evidence you'll let the Defence have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I think in some cases what we will be doing primarily the 89(F) statement is going to be the statement that perhaps we propose for a 92 bis witness, their prior ICTY statement in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there is, I suppose, one issue that we mustn't lose sight of and that is that you have certain disclosure obligations which include disclosure of statements within time-scales which are already passed. Now obviously if you prepare a statement in a different form which is saying more or less what has been disclosed before, no issue arises. But insofar as far these statements go into territory which has not been disclosed before, then there will be issues over the permission of the Chamber for that to happen. So you should be conscious of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We certainly understand that, Your Honour. I can tell my experience in another case where this happened, and I think it's happened in other cases in this Tribunal. Witnesses arrived here, and perhaps the last time they talked to anyone in the OTP about this was five years ago when their statement was taken. They may bring documents that we've never seen before. They may talk about something that they weren't asked. They may expand on something that was in a prior statement. In that other case where this arose, we took down that information during the proofing session, we labelled a supplemental information form. And if it were something that we proposed to try and lead in court, we gave it to the Defence as soon as we had it in hand and then we left it up to the discretion of the Court whether or not they would permit it because it was so recent. In some cases, the solution was to give the Defence additional time, to delay cross-examination, whatever the Court deemed fair and appropriate in the circumstances, and we would propose to proceed the same way here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Does any Defence counsel wish to say anything on this matter? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. What I would like to say is that at least our team of the Defence would prefer to have the complete statements of the witnesses. We appreciate the efforts of the learned friends from the opposite, but if we talk about Mr. Stoparic, it's obvious that he was cross-examined on other issues where his credibility was challenged and we would maybe like to challenge his credibility through his testimony regarding some other issues like Bosnia or Trnovo, and he doesn't -- is not maybe directly connected with Kosovo but is connected with his credibility. So our position is that we would like to have complete statements of this witness and every other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then we can choose what to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I may have misunderstood, but I thought Mr. Hannis was indicating that that material would already have been disclosed. Let's check with him. My understanding - but please correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Hannis - is that you're saying that the complete statements would already have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There were three separate ICTY statements from which this 89(F) statement is composed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the material is already available, I think, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we would like to have is all his statements. Also statements given to the Belgrade court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those that we have have been disclosed. I think we do have his statements from his testimony in a case in the Belgrade war crimes prosecution court, and that has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, we don't have those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would invite you to get together after this hearing to clarify that, but the will of the Prosecution is that you should have them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll contact after this session. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply make the concluding comment that I made earlier but I think it's worth making again, that I hope the Defence will endeavour to do something similar when it comes to presenting Defence evidence, insofar as that turns out to be possible. The next item is headed: Requirement for evidence in private or closed session. There is a rule on this matter, which is Rule 79. It's the will of the Trial Chamber to endeavour to conduct the whole of the trial in public. Now, there are inevitable exceptions to that that will arise along the way, but we will not readily depart from that. And the rule, Rule 79, requires that when there is a closed session the Trial Chamber shall make public the reason for its orders -- or the reasons for its order. As a result, it will be necessary whenever you invite the Chamber to go into what you describe as private or closed session for you to explain why. Now, I appreciate that sometimes a full explanation requires you to enter into the area that has to remain private. So within reason you must state why so that we can point to the reason that we have for granting the application. My understanding of this rule is that closed session is a form of evidence in which the public is entirely excluded; they can neither hear nor see what's going on because these blinds also come down. And the modified version of that, which is described as being excluded from all or part of the proceedings, has come to be known as private session and generally involves the blinds remaining up so that the outside world can see what's happening without hearing what's going on, and that's how we will apply these terms in the conduct of the trial. That takes us to may turn out to be the most controversial part of this agenda, which is Rule 73 bis. I think there are too many items probably listed. The first one I don't think arises here. I don't think we're in a position at this stage to call upon you to shorten the estimated length of examination-in-chief for some witnesses, but, as you know, the Trial Chamber has an inherent power to do that at any stage in the proceedings, and that's one power that won't be exercised at this stage. And similarly, the last one listed, to direct the Prosecution to select counts on the indictment which the -- that doesn't arise in this type of case. It arises in different situations. So that -- you can take your pen through that. The issues are therefore those in 73 bis (C) and (D). It might help if I give you -- I'll say something about time; it might help focus the debate on the other issues. I think the history of the Tribunal probably drives you to the conclusion that some limitation on time will be necessary to reach our goal in a reasonable time. However, I've had an opportunity over almost two years now to experience working with the personnel who are involved in this case, and my initial inclination with which I think my colleagues are prepared to go along at my persuasion, is to let it run and see what happens and to trust you, as responsible counsel, to keep this case within bounds. But I recognise it may be necessary, as we move along, to make orders that sort out any kinks that may crop up. The Appeals Chamber has recently issued a judgement which approves an approach, a broad-brush approach, that allows the Defence en bloc the equivalent time to cross-examine that the Prosecution has. Let's wait and see if it's necessary to take that sort of action in this case and let's see if we can't actually manage to do it in a responsible way that recognises that for some witnesses a bit more -- or maybe even substantially more is required and for other witnesses, not even as much is required. Now, if anyone dissents from that, please tell me now. Okay -- Oh, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I -- I don't dissent. Actually, I'm very happy about that. The point I wanted to make, it relates to scheduling of witnesses. If there were -- if we had some idea of an outward limit on cross-examination, as a general rule it would help us in determining how many witnesses we should have in hand for each week. And I understand this may be something that we'll get into as we go along and we'll get a feel for, okay, well, if it's Mr. So-and-so is cross-examining and he says it's going to take an hour, I should count on two; and if it's so-and-so and he says an hour, that's an hour; and if so-and-so says two, I can take 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's also the related point that you've made that because you lead evidence in writing there may be a bit of an imbalance created in that and inevitably the cross-examination will take longer than the time that you've take. I can see that. I also think that there may be quite a difference between the proportion of time that the Defence need for cross-examination and the proportion of time they need to present their own case. And it's impossible at this stage to make sensible judgements about those matters. I don't know -- I really don't know the circumstances of any other current trial with which this -- you could attempt to compare this. All I know is that in this case we're all talking about the same crime base, whereas we may be talking about quite discrete evidence going to criminal responsibility, although there may be a measure of overlap, a significant measure of overlap because of the joint criminal enterprise. So I at the moment can't come to any firm view about time. But I think initially, Mr. Hannis, you're probably going to have to err on the side of caution and have more witnesses than even your better judgement dictates you should have available. You're going to have a week, roughly, to experience it. In the second week of the trial -- it may be a bit longer than the average week, too. So after a couple of weeks, you might be in a bit better position to judge. I don't think I can give you more guidance on that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And I guess I'm sort of trying to foreshadow the possibility that there may come a week where on Friday morning at 10.00 I discover that we've finished with all the witnesses we had for that week because things went faster. I would ask for some patience from the Court. And perhaps if that does occur, on those days we could deal perhaps with outstanding administrative housekeeping matters which always seem to arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And hopefully if that does happen, it will be an indication that we've gotten ahead of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope so, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that diverts attention to the other methods that are available for bringing the trial itself within narrower bounds than is presently -- than are presently heralded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one thing in that regard, Your Honour. Perhaps when we provide the Defence a list of our witnesses for the next week or the next two weeks, in some cases if there's a particular witness they think may require extra cross-examination because it has special pertinence to their accused or some particularly controversial issue, if they could advise us of that, to the extent possible, that would help me with my scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think the way to address the other methods that are open to the Court is perhaps to invite Mr. Visnjic to address -- yeah, it was your motion in relation to the number of crime sites. Perhaps you would wish to address the Chamber on how we might approach that issue. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Frankly, Your Honours, we had a little bit of a debate in the Defence team as to whether to file our suggestion at all because Your Honour at the last 65 ter conference had already invited the Prosecutor to seriously consider this question and to come up with some ideas, perhaps today, in terms of limiting the number of crime sites in the indictment. But we thought ultimately that Your Honour wouldn't mind if we joined you in the invitation to the Prosecutors, because that's all we meant by that suggestion that we filed. We -- there actually, there is one error in that motion. It talks about 32 separate crime sites; that's for the deportations, the alleged deportations, and murders. There's actually 38. If you go through the indictment, there are 38 separate incidents alleged of deportation and murder in various parts of the indictment. We came up with a ten figure. How did we come up with a ten figure? Frankly, Your Honour, we plucked it out of the air. It's simply a basis for discussion. As I understand the rule, the Prosecutor is invited to consider this and because it's a very serious and important matter for the Prosecutor, and I would think that the Prosecutor might -- surely has some ideas on what at least the irreducible minimum would be for the presentation of their case, which perhaps they will have -- with Your Honour's guidance, perhaps they'll enlighten us with that this afternoon. But we didn't -- that ten doesn't have any magic to it. We're trying to come up with some figure that we think might be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I have allowed a significantly larger total of actual crime sites or locations, something approaching the high 70s. Can you help me in how we appear to have -- I know you've had some discussion about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the difference in our respective approaches to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed this with -- Mr. Visnjic and I discussed this yesterday briefly with Mr. Boas, and we simply went to that part of the indictment, for example, which alleges the deportations in Count 1. And we started with number (a) -- by the way, I'm still a rookie in this case, so forgive my pronunciations here. But the crime sites listed (a) -- (a) and then little (i), we went through all of those, and then we went through all of the crime sites mentioned in the murder counts of the indictment. And unless my mathematics are woefully incorrect, we came up with a total of 38 separate incidents, as alleged in those portions of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: To be more precise, Your Honour, for example in 72(a) in the deportation count, in the village of Celina is mentioned. In 72(a)(i) the village of Nogavac is mentioned. In (b) it's Pirane, and so on. That's how we came up with the 38 figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your approach to this is to invite the Prosecution to simply identify ten sites that they would wish to lead evidence about as representative of the indictment as a whole and confine the crime base part of the case to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I have to say in all frankness that -- again, the ten -- it could have been 15, it could have been 20. I mean, really, I think it would be unfair to burden the Prosecutor at this point with a figure of ten. I mean, that's at least the way the Ojdanic team feels about it. Until they've expressed themselves. And needless to say, if they can take ten crime sites and make those representative of the case as a whole, obviously under Your Honours' guidance, then I think that would be a very fine way to proceed. But I -- again, without having heard the Prosecution's position on this, I hesitate to have any kind of certainty on this issue because it's a very complex issue and it goes to the heart of what the Prosecutor has to present. And I think in fairness to them -- and all I'm doing, Your Honour, is picking up on what you've already said at the 65 ter conference. And, again, all we did, all the Ojdanic team did was join in your invitation to the Prosecutor to come up with something a lot more reasonable than the rather staggering array of crime sites that we have to face in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Between just the 72(a), if you just look at that -- it's the very first one, just as an example, I have Celina and Prizren, I suppose two crime sites in the one -- well, maybe Celina is the only crime site, but Prizren, as you'll see, is mentioned. And then in (i), 72(a)(i) I've got Nogavac, Bela Crkva, Brestovac, and Velika Krusa. Now, you've treated 72(a)(i) as really one, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I suppose, Your Honour, if we were at -- went at it with great mathematical precision, you're absolutely right, and we'd hit every single thing mentioned in every part of the indictment. 38 was just sort of our way of saying that there's 38 different paragraphs alleged regarding crime sites. And again, ten was also a figure used simply as a basis for discussion and to get the issue on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Now, does any other Defence counsel wish to say anything before I ask Mr. Hannis to reply? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would first suggest to the Court that this is not a matter that necessarily lends itself easily to a mathematical calculation. I would indicate that my count of the sites and incidents we are talking about is different from either of the two figures that were mentioned before, and I'll explain how I did my counting, if I may, Your Honour. In my view, for deportation -- and I should say that deportation is a crime that you can't necessarily limit to one site because on the evidence you'll hear in this case somebody in Celina village was marched to Prizren, that they were temporarily located somewhere, later on they were removed from there, marched down the road, and eventually out of the country. So we have these operations where the forces are moving through an area, and we might talk about five or six villages on a certain day. And one witness may be able to speak to five or six because he saw what happened in front of him, he left his and went to a third, et cetera. By my count we had 13 municipalities that we referred to as deportation municipalities. And I counted within those 13 municipalities 20 separate incidents, and that's basically a count of the paragraphs, paragraph 72, 72(a), et cetera, is how I got my numbers. And then for the killing sites -- we referred to killing sites or killing incidents. For killing sites, we had 11 separate sites with 14 incidents. And the way I came to that count, Your Honour, was because in the municipality of Kacanik we listed four separate killings on four separate dates, and that's why we have 14 incidents for 11 sites. I should say also there's some overlap between the alleged deportation sites and the killing sites. Of the 11 killing sites, three - Racak, Padaliste, and Dubrava prison - do not have a related municipality site alleging deportations. So reversed of our 14 -- or of our 13 municipalities involving deportation, six of them had related killing sites, seven have no related killing sites alleged in connection with them. We did hear the comments of your principal Legal Officer in the 65 ters, indicating that we might anticipate an invitation from Your Honours to consider reducing our case. And we understood -- we saw the Defence motion. We were -- I guess we were expecting this perhaps to proceed a little bit differently, but it is difficult, Your Honour, to pick a number that will necessarily be representative of all the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify one thing with you. You say that three of the sites - that's the killing sites - don't have related deportation sites, but when you turn to the deportation sites you say that seven of them don't have related killing sites. Now, it's difficult to match these figures in my mind. Can you clarify the relationship there for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, because, for example, Orahovac municipality, which is one of our alleged deportation sites, it has two separate killings sites: Bela Crkva and Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Djakovica has two killing sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, doesn't what you've just said point up an important factor? This case would be seen as, at the very least, a case of ethnic manipulation, if it's not ethnic cleansing. So deportation and forcible transfer is an essential ingredient of the case. You then tell me that three of the killings are not -- do not seem to be related to deportation events. Is there not something to be said for them not forming part of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly there's something to be said for that, Your Honour, but I don't think that necessarily leads you to an inescapable conclusion. Part of our argument in this case is that some of the killings occurred to cause terror in the community and to cause people to leave. You don't have to kill them all if by killing a few you can get the rest to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But one of the things -- one of the possibilities here is that the position is reviewed at a later stage. You have the power of the right to come back and ask the Chamber to review this decision, depending on developments in the case. So it's not a final decision if we make it today. But I wonder if there isn't something to be said for looking at removing these three for the moment and seeing how things go in the presentation of the case, because it inevitably won't go quite as well as you hope. But if it does go well or even better than you hope, then there would be plenty of scope for you to apply to reintroduce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, Your Honour. I guess as a prosecutor, and you understand an old prosecutor who has been dealing with carrying the burden of beyond a reasonable doubt for many years, it turns us into Nervous Nellies, if you will, and we're always anxious that we need more than maybe we really do. And I can tell you that in the course of this case as things go along, we would be keeping a close eye of how things were developing in our view. If we felt that after presentation on five or six municipalities we felt confident that we had established a pattern, then we would certainly be bearing in mind that now maybe we don't need to proceed with those that were scheduled later on in our case. And I certainly would rather proceed that way, with keeping everything in and having a chance to reduce it later, rather than having it reduced now and then asking you to put it in later. One of my reasons for that, Your Honour, if I were on the other side of the room as Defence counsel and we had proceeded in that fashion and the Prosecution decided that he needed more and asked you to reinstate or let us have some of the old counts back in, at Defence table I would say, well, Your Honour, I thought those were gone. And those first ten witnesses, I didn't ask any questions related to that and I would have if I had known. And then we have to decide whether or not we need to bring those witnesses back to be cross-examined about those things. So that's a practical concern I have about proceeding in that fashion. One other thing I want to indicate to Your Honour. In that regard, given the comments that we got during the 65 ter and in light of the Defence motion asking you to invoke Rule 73 and call upon us or to fix the number of sites at some number lower, we have scheduled certain municipalities at the end of our evidence in light of what we were told were areas that you saw to perhaps be outside the temporal core of our indictment and perhaps outside the principal theory of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the two I mentioned or suggested should be mentioned were Racak and Dubrava prison. And certainly in relation to Prizren, it's difficult to see how that fits the pattern, albeit there is activity in the neighbourhood. Racak of course is divorced temporally from the other events. But anyway, these -- I'm very grateful for your comments, Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if -- if the Trial Chamber is minded to determine that the trial should proceed on crime sites representative of the conflict -- representative of the indictment as presented, and to decide that on the face of it that objective can be achieved without proceeding in relation to Racak, Padaliste, and Dubrava, the Dubrava prison, does any Defence counsel have any submission to make to the contrary, bearing in mind that depending on how the case develops there is always the possibility of re-introduction and that even the Bench itself may feel not in a position to fully reflect events because of the way the evidence goes without looking again at these incidents. But on the face of it, as presented to us at the moment, it does seem that the case can be adequately presented on an entirely complete and representative basis without these three events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the decision of the Trial Chamber - and this will need to be issued in writing for the avoidance of any doubt and for complete clarity - will be to confine the trial to a varying number of events, varying between the low 30s and the high 70s, but excluding these three particular ones, which will be more specifically defined in the order, always recognising the further provisions of Rule 73 bis (D), which could result in these ultimately nevertheless becoming part of the trial. Now, our inclination, in light of coming to that view, is that there's no need to limit the number of witnesses that can be led in the case, unless someone has any particular submission to make to the contrary. All right. That, I think, completes the consideration of 73 bis and takes us to the issues concerning the conduct of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- on to that, may I ask a question or make a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to your decision, I guess I have a question about what "representative" means in this context, representative of the case and what's -- may I ask what the Trial Chamber's view of that is or your definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We consider that the case that you seek to present based on deportations, killings, and persecutions is adequately covered by the indictment without these three events being part of the trial, and that's not to say that they are also -- that they in some way are not representative of the case. But on the face of it they're the clear examples of events which aren't as representative of the case that you're presenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- as the rest are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand and I understand how you reached that conclusion. My other question is reading Rule 73 (D) indicates that the Trial Chamber can, first of all, invite us to reduce the number of counts which we've decided doesn't apply in this circumstance. The other is that you may fix a number of crime sites or incidents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's because that has to be done in a positive way that I will be -- we will be issuing a written determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. I don't read from the rule itself. It says you may fix a number of sites but not necessarily the particular sites. Not that I necessarily have any quarrel with the choices that you've made, Your Honour, but I just note that from my reading of the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that will be the way that we will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's pointless -- well, are you suggesting -- if you're suggesting that we don't have power ourselves to identify the sites, that that provision only allows us to identify a number and leave it to your discretion, then I would need to hear more from you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think a strict reading of the language reads that way, but as a practical matter in real life, I don't think that's a very -- a very good rule. For example, you know, we have 13 sites, and I say, okay, you can tell me to lead ten. Well, I can take the three sites that had three victims each and it really wouldn't amount to a very big reduction in the case, for example. So I think what you've chosen to do is -- makes more sense, but I telling you that's my reading of the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're reading -- your interpretation would be stronger if the word was "the number of crime sites or incidents which are reasonably representative of the crimes charged." When you say "a number," then that means there's an element of discretion involved in identifying which ones. And it wouldn't, I think, make much sense to have a rule that left it to -- entirely to the Prosecutor to do that and then leave everyone dissatisfied that in fact he hadn't chosen a representative sample. I think if that was the interpretation that was favoured here, then I would regard it as a two-stage exercise, that the next stage would be for you to tell me the sites that you think are reasonably representative of the crimes charged, and we would then decide whether to accept that version or not. Now, if you want to go through that exercise, then perhaps we should. But if on the other hand you see sense in what we're doing, then it may not make any sense to go through another chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think in the particular circumstances I do see sense in the choices you have made. But I do want to indicate that, you know, part of our problem with certain aspects of Rule 73 are -- is that we see it perhaps as being ultra vires of the Statute and allowing the judiciary to intrude in the area of what should be the Prosecution's bailiwick. And the Prosecution should be in the best position to determine what's representative of their case. That's just a general proposition I'm making, Your Honour, and not disagreeing with what you've done in this particular situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're telling me that the decision is likely to be challenged, then obviously we might approach it in a different way, but you must have got the favour by now, Mr. Hannis, that practicality is fairly high in my criteria for applying rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have seen that, Your Honour, and I respect that and admire that. And as far as whether there would be any decision by our office to appeal a decision on this matter, I can't tell you at this point. It's something we would have to have discussions about. But I see the reasons for you making the choices you've made, and I'm ready to proceed with the rest of the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one other issue's been raised with me, Mr. Hannis. Your witnesses next week --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- do deal with Padaliste, but they must be wider than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That particular witness is pretty much the Padaliste killing site, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The third witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which witness, the third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Imeraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Imeraj, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And in light of the 92 bis decision, I think the first couple of witnesses at the beginning of the week in August when we return after the break also relate to Padaliste. That schedule wasn't made in anticipation of this event, Your Honour, I can promise you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hannis, all I can do in the circumstances is invite you to review your witness list as expeditiously as you can and decide what changes you can make to make things progress smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have plenty of time to do something about the first week in August. My concern is next week; it may be difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, do your best, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to ask if we can have this amended list from the Prosecution so we don't have to wait for the files, so that we can have a look at the amendments as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Hannis will take note of what you say. Now, the last section of the agenda is certain practical issues relating to the conduct of the trial. Through the e-court training recently, we've all learned that most documents can be produced electronically. This Chamber is going to try to work electronically as far as possible, but undoubtedly there will be documents of odd shapes and sizes which need to be here in hard copy. And you may, indeed, find it more convenient for the presentation of your case, your examination or cross-examination, to have hard copy in the hands of the Judges. It's a matter for you to determine. I'm just anxious to ensure that thought's given to these issues before you come into court and we don't have unnecessary interruptions through the absence of necessary material. The second matter listed was the arrangement for intermitting witnesses. Do you find that one convenient, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's agreeable with us. We would indicate -- we would ask that Your Honour allow us flexibility in the sense of scheduling witnesses two months out that there will be a lot of changes in the course of time. But we will try to give as much notice, particularly for experts or significant insiders, internationals, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doing it monthly should allow you plenty of flexibility to re-arrange and plenty of time for others to be alerted to any changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, Your Honour, again is the issue of it will take us a while, I think, for -- for me to get a feel for how long cross-examination will be in order to know how many witnesses and how long ahead of time they need to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the -- the next subject was procedure for cross-examination. That simply is a reflection of something we discussed earlier at either a Status Conference or a 65 ter conference. The idea that Defence counsel would try, as far as possible, to identify a lead counsel in relation to matters and others would endeavour to keep their cross confined to particular additional factors that might affect their respective client or they feel have been overlooked by the lead counsel appointed. Now, you did indicate to me at the time that you thought that would be a way of proceeding. Is that still your plan or has that plan changed? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We've -- as we previously discussed, that is our intention, to proceed in this way -- in one of two ways: The normal order of cross-examination would follow the order in the indictment, but if there is unanimous agreement among us to change that order, we would announce that to the Chamber immediately examination-in-chief. That decision would be made outside the court, so no time would be wasted with consulting -- it would be prearranged. On the clear understanding that each and every accused retains the right to cross-examine every witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Previously in a domestic context when I've been faced with this situation, there's been some concern that by changing the order it can cause prejudice to an accused. That only happens, however, where there's a conflict of interest, and at the moment it's not immediately obvious that there is a conflict of interest among the accused, although there may be one -- I think I'm wrong in saying that. There may be one potential conflict. If that were to be in your minds, I would understand why you would stick rigidly to the order and let each counsel indicate, in order, his position. But insofar as you're able to agree no conflict arises and you have a common interest, then I would welcome a cross-examination -- it's going to help us as well if you concentrate your efforts in one person. So that's very helpful. You'll bear in mind also the discussion at yesterday's -- yesterday morning's meeting about the translation of material, both for cross-examination purposes and for the presentation of the Defence case. If you know now that you've got material which will need to be translated for some -- for some stage of the trial, then it should be in the hands of CLSS now so that they can do it at their leisure, as it were. They indicated they do get gaps in the schedule and then they get overwhelmed, and they want to make use of the gaps. So this is a case, I think, in which assistance could be given to them by the production of material at an early stage for translation purposes. And if there are translation problems a year down the line, the Trial Chamber will probably want to know why, bearing in mind the time that we've got and the notice that we've had of the system that's operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
