utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In relation to cross-examination, may I ask what the Trial Chamber's vision was about re-examination by the Prosecution. Time limits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's consistent with encouraging you to restrict your examination-in-chief and to use written material where appropriate to recognise that it may be necessary to spend more time from time to time in re-examination just to be fair. So I had envisaged that we might find that the concentration in this case in relation to a large number of witnesses would be in cross and re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Re-examination is to be allowed wherever it's necessary. I mean, that's something to be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, the particular position of Mr. Pavkovic in the absence of Mr. Ackerman, I undertook that I would raise the question of the Prosecution trying to avoid the leading of evidence that would be particularly controversial for Mr. Pavkovic's case during that period. Now, that period may be extensive. It could extend up to the end of August, I think. So let's hear what Mr. Hannis has to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were previously aware that Mr. Ackerman wouldn't be here for the first week of July and -- of the trial. And we changed one witness because of Mr. Ackerman's concern. Now we understand it will be a longer period of time. I haven't looked at our list to the end of the month of August to see if we put on somebody that might cause a problem or be, in his view, particularly controversial. We will try and adjust to that, but as it goes on longer it becomes more and more difficult. I would indicate that some witnesses may speak in general about the VJ or the army, which certainly relates to General Pavkovic. But his superior and his subordinate are here with counsel who will be cross-examining, and Mr. Aleksic is here, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take that point, though, but I think what you should do, Mr. -- bearing in mind that this is actually six separate trials, albeit they're rolled together for practical reasons, I think you owe it to Mr. Aleksic in the situation to discuss directly with him the plans for the leading of evidence to enable him to make any specific comments he wishes to make about individual witnesses perhaps being programmed differently, so that at least you can take account of that. I acknowledge that at the end of the day it's for you to decide. But I think Mr. Ackerman will certainly be reassured if he knows that there's going to be this personal exchange that will ensure that the comments that are made on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic are taken account of before you actually finalise the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have borne that in mind and will continue to do so. And it's not our intention to call any witness in the month of August who had 20 face-to-face meetings with General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. There is such a witness, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was thinking, I wonder if we have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fila, that takes us to two items intimated by you. Can we deal, first of all, with the -- what's called the selection of evidence. You mentioned it briefly earlier as an issue that you wanted to address the Chamber on. I think it was relating to whether hearsay evidence should be taken account of where there was some direct evidence that could have been brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, since I've been doing this job, this question has been raised and I think the generations to come after me will deal with this question. It's a very interesting question, hearsay evidence, and I am not one of the people who believe that such witnesses should not be heard. I personally belong to the French school, and that's where I studied and so on, and there was this example. If a house is on fire and if a person burning in a house says, I was burned by such and such a person, of course this person cannot be heard because he never survived. So of course there is going to be a hearsay witness who's going to say that such and such a person was burned. So this is from the second year of law school, this example that I'm referring to. So we've got something similar. I'm expressing my concern. The Office of the Prosecution and others often in the documents that they present, you see a statement: I talked to such and such and such and such a person, that's what they said to me, and that suffices, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, whereas the survivors are alive and well. Let us take, for example, Mr. Dimitrijevic. They are invoking what he said. He held the same position like Mr. Vasiljevic. Mr. Dimitrijevic is making statements to the press in Belgrade, he's strolling around Belgrade, nobody's calling him as a witness, they're just calling Vasiljevic. At one meeting I mentioned Mr. Philip Coo. He is referring to some records of this so-called Joint Command, and you never called the person who actually wrote those records who has a name and surname. He's a general, he's in Belgrade. No one called him, either in the Milosevic case or in this case, and I really do not understand why. I'm sorry, I've been going on forever, and I know that there is limited time only. I'm expressing the following concern. We want to have a public trial indeed; we don't want to evade that. You said it was the intention of this Chamber to have this trial be carried out in public as much as possible, to have the smallest number of private sessions. So let us call a person who has what he has to say, rather than bring in a clerk or somebody else who just heard about something, whereas this person is alive and well and can be made available. After all, the Court can also resort to subpoenas. So let us hear exactly who said what. This takes us nowhere. Let us simplify things. Let us just call the investigators of the Prosecution. Let them tell us who they interviewed, who they heard, and what they heard from them, and then the trial will be over in three or four days. I understand that if you have people that you cannot reach for some reason -- well, in that case, I fully accept the right of my learned friend to call hearsay evidence or if somebody died, like Rugova, or, for example, if Mr. Clark is not allowed to testify because of his own state, and then the French Ambassador, Mr. Keller who said this, who said that, but I never heard Keller say what he had actually said. So there are objective things that have to be taken into account. However, when we have a person who is alive and well, why not bring him in? And why can we not see whether he actually said that and, if so, in what context. And, you know, it's 1999, whereas now is the year of 2006, so things fade from one's memory. Anyway, whatever this Trial Chamber decides, I will be satisfied, but in all trials I've had so far there was that problem, and I claim that generations to come will have to deal with this. What is the value of that kind of evidence if the actual person is still accessible who can speak for himself? That's what I meant. Thank you. That's the question that I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber to look at. We can reach any kind of agreement, but we simply have to know what the rules are going to be. Thank you. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any Defence counsel wish to add anything to that? Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, it might be a little premature at this point, Your Honour, but I was intending to raise a similar issue really with respect to the two witnesses Sandra Mitchell and Fred Abrahams who are going to be testifying next week. And the reason I was going to bring it up is due in no small part to comments made by Your Honour on March 30th, 2006 at a 65 ter conference. I wasn't in the case at that point, but I do have a transcript of the conference. And you'll recall, Your Honour, that Fred Abrahams and Sandra Mitchell -- Abrahams was with Human Rights Watch, Sandra Mitchell is OSCE, and they both -- their organisations have written books which Mr. Hannis and his colleagues want to introduce, I believe, into evidence, one called "Under Orders," and one called "As Seen, As Told." Rather extensive reports on the situation in Kosovo from March to June of 1999. And, Your Honour, with your permission, read very briefly, what Your Honour said at the 65 ter conference. You said: "Now, the bulk of his evidence," meaning Abrahams, "is hearsay evidence. He's recounting what other people have gathered as information from their contact with witnesses either at the borders or near to the borders of Kosovo. Is that right?" And of course Mr. Hannis agrees and says that he was with the human rights -- Human Watch organisation. And you said, Your Honour: "And there is a very little amount" -- "There's a very little amount of direct testimony from him, direct knowledge of events. Is that correct?" Mr. Hannis said: "I think that's a fair statement. He may address some matters regarding 1998. Now, that's a liver issue in connection with our indictment as well." Liver, l-i-v-e-r. And then Your Honour said: "I don't think I'm overstepping the mark when I say you obviously have to have particular regard to the value of that type of evidence. In the trial of Milosevic, we had that evidence from Human Rights Watch and we also had evidence from the OSCE I've seen. I was told that no one has really applied or made a determination yet of the weight that will ultimately be given to that evidence, if indeed it is admitted at the trial, so thought may have yet to be given to these issues even before the trial starts." Now, Mr. Fila of course has expressed himself on the issue. And I'm simply asking, given the rules of evidence in the Tribunal, again which I don't pretend in any way, shape or form to be an expert, but having read that -- you know, I'm used to rules of evidence in a book that thick. And the rules of evidence here are simply Your Honours can admit whatever relevance [sic] you want as long as it's not outweighed by the prejudicial impact. But it is very disconcerting for the Defence -- I think I speak for all my colleagues. Well, I'll at least speak to the Ojdanic team. Here are two major books, if Your Honours do admit them into evidence, which are based entirely really on hearsay. I think that Abrahams and Mitchell have just a very, very tiny amount of personal knowledge on any of the events set forth in those books, and those books being based almost exclusively on hearsay contains some very damaging information. And I think that there's an argument that can be made that it would really be unfair to admit these books or, at the very least, to give the books very little weight in your consideration of the case. I'm simply raising this as an issue now to see if it might be appropriate for resolution by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sepenuk, I don't think that issue can be resolved until the witness actually goes into the witness box and we begin to hear the nature of the evidence that the witness is giving. What I was doing in March was alerting the Prosecution to something that I expected to be raised and about which I have some concern, most particularly the weight that might be given to that evidence. But I did leave open, as you heard, the possibility that it may not even be admitted. These are decisions that can only be taken once a Trial Chamber is gathered to deal with it, and my colleagues haven't heard sufficient submissions to deal with these issues finally, nor have they I, think, enough knowledge at the moment of the content of the material. That will emerge once we see the witness indicate the nature of the material first. Once we've heard that and if an objection is taken, then we'll have to look at that particular objection in its context and decide whether, in fact, it's such that it has to be rejected, in spite of the weakness of the Rules here, or whether it is a question of the weight to be given in the light of the fact that the Defence have an opportunity themselves to lead contradictory evidence. So these are things we'll attack when they arise in the course of next week. But on this separate question, which is -- well, I suppose it's a related question, but it's a much more general one that Mr. Fila makes that if there is somebody actually alive who can speak to something, is it permissible -- and that person's identified, which may not always be the case with the OSCE and Human Rights Watch evidence. But in the more significant case of a witness who is speaking specifically about what happened to someone else and that someone else is still there, or is speaking about what that person said, should the hearsay evidence be admitted at all. That's the question he's raising. Now, do you have anything to add on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, I -- you know, I -- I certainly -- do you want to -- do you want me to -- I certainly agree with the thrust and the spirit and the philosophy and the theory of what Mr. Fila has to say. I realise that as a practical matter these are sometimes very difficult questions. But I think it's incontrovertibly true when there's a witness available to testify, that's the way that we ought to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Hannis, do you want to respond to these submissions? I don't think you need to deal with the question of Abrahams and Mitchell, but on the other point about leading hearsay where everyone knows that the person who actually was directly involved in available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the rule in this Tribunal is that hearsay is admissible. There's nothing in the Rules that says when hearsay involves a situation where the actual speaker is available that the hearsay is not admissible. It may be a factor that would give the hearsay less weight, knowing that the actual declarant is available. But, as Your Honour knows, there can be all kinds of reasons that that individual may not be appearing before the Tribunal. We may know where somebody is, but actually being able to get them here or, once having them here, being able to rely on them testifying and testifying completely, truthfully, accurately, is another consideration as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think -- Mr. -- sorry, do you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sorry, I'm taking up more of your time. Mr. Hannis, sorry, I'm addressing you directly. I'm not referring to hundreds of witnesses and hundreds of sites. Of course I don't want to burden you with thousands of witnesses who will be saying the same thing. I think that perhaps you understand full well what I'm telling you. I took the example of Mr. Dimitrijevic just by way of an example. These are people who are very significant for your case, as far as this hearsay evidence is concerned. You know, I don't really think that the truth is compounded if 60 people tell it. It's just a waste of time, or perhaps I'm just stupid for not having understood it, and maybe you have to call 60 people to tell me the same thing. But anyway, why is an important person not brought in? What was he, the chief of counter-intelligence, whatever at that time? It's not some little captain or lieutenant or whatever -- well, you've been calling captains, but never mind. This is an important man. I'm trying to say in that kind of situation I don't think it's a good idea, and I think that the Court should make the Prosecutor call that man. Let's see if he really said that. Well, you know, if he's evading this Court, well, you can have him brought in. Any court, I mean even in our parts, has ways and means of bringing someone in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With the permission of the chair, I would just like to make a small comment with all respect to your learning and to your reasoning. Well, of course the rule says hearsay is not excluded here. But elsewhere in different other jurisprudences there are exceptions where hearsay is allowed, confessional statements and the rest of it. The learned counsel had himself pointed out that if somebody's saying, I'm burning because of this and somebody else is quoting him, that will be inadmissible. No. When something is said in a stress while the -- even overtakes the person or the circumstances overtakes the person and somebody hears him, to that extent it is admissible. So the question would be, as you very well said, and we enjoyed your very learned discourse, sir. The point would be that these are difficult questions, and every situation will itself say whether this is to be excluded or not, whether it at all has a weight or it is to be it's not worth the paper on which it is to be written. Again, you also have to kindly see that you have to point out while we proceed further and the case develops, that here is a person who is available and who is purposely not being brought with a design. So that will be something which will give you a very extraordinary -- will provide extraordinary strength to your argument and for us to take a decision. But at this stage I think it will be rather very difficult to say this is -- I'm sorry to say it will be a bit hypothetical, to say that this to be included. But what you have said should also provide the other side with a thought that -- that these objections are forthcoming and also with a thought that if they are capable of producing the primary evidence, then they may exclude the secondary evidence, which has always been the law. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can take it that the Trial Chamber -- the rest of the Chamber takes the same view as Judge Chowhan on this. We appreciate your cri de coeur, we appreciate your warning to the Prosecution about the arguments that undoubtedly will be advanced in due course if this happens. But I think the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, and indeed your submission recognises this, Mr. Fila, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in principle allows for the admission of hearsay evidence even in the sort of situation you identify applying to the evidence of Vasiljevic. It follows that it's always going to be a matter to be determined according to the individual circumstances affecting that witness. And, as Judge Chowhan says, we will need to make these decisions as and when the problems arise. But we are grateful to you for your general submission. And some might even hope that your wish will eventually be granted, not just in generations to come. Now, we will need to break again, I'm afraid. I don't expect to need more than a half an hour of another session. We'll resume at -- let's try to resume at ten past -- 4.15 then. We'll resume at 4.15. The matters outstanding -- the other matter you listed, Mr. Fila, was the question of a Kosovo site visit and you can address that when we return. And the one other matter I have relates to any order that we might make about just the practical conduct of the trial, and I will raise a number of individual but brief matters in that connection. Is there any other issue that counsel on either side anticipates raising in the balance of the hearing? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One, Your Honour, relates to a matter of scheduling because of a story that appeared in the Politika newspaper on July 4th concerning the health issue of one of our accused. And I don't know if Your Honours were aware of that, but we can discuss it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't. And Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There are a couple of matters I would like to raise concerning transportation to and from the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you need to raise that with the Trial Chamber, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with that then. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just have a small remark to make in relation to the schedule over the summer. I just want to say it for the sake of the transcript because of some of the decisions that are to be taken by the Registrar. I would like to do that at the very end; it won't take more than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the subject of the site visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours. We tried to raise that in relation to the Bosnian cases many times, but it wasn't possible at the time, considering the mood that prevailed about Omarska and everything else. The security situation at the time is such that the Chamber would be safe, but we ourselves would not; the Chamber would be safe, though. We think -- I've lived long enough, after all. There is no risk that I would not be prepared to assume. I'm prepared to assume this risk, so are all of us; the important thing is for you and the Prosecutors to be safe. We probably have reason to fear a number of things in our own country, but you don't. I think it would be a good idea to look at several places, at least, those selected by the Chamber. I think that would be a good idea. I'm not about to start discussing that. It's just like the previous thing that I told you. I just wanted to give some sort of a warning or some food for thought. Although this is not part of our agenda, something I would like to ask you on behalf of all the accused. The trial begins on the 7th of August. Pursuant to your order, they should be back by the 31st of July. What we would like to ask you is to move that to the 4th of July [as interpreted] and then Mr. Hannis's deadlines would also be by the 4th of July [as interpreted], in as far as that is possible, of course. These are the two things I wanted to ask you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dealing with the second one first, it's just impractical, I'm afraid. The arrangements within the Detention Unit are such that return has to be on the 31st. I understand your concern and the desire to have that period of freedom, but it was seriously considered at the time and for practical reasons that's the decision that was made and will remain. On the question of the visit, just let me consider one thing with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber had -- did give some thought to the question of visiting the area. Judge Kamenova has direct experience of Serbia. I have a very limited recent experience, as I explained to you before. And Judge Chowhan has none. And he's been somewhat concerned about that and whether that needs to be rectified. But we've decided that if it does need to be rectified, it should be in the context of exploring evidence which parties have identified as needing further consideration in light of a locus inspection. Whether that is necessary will depend on the circumstances at the time. I would imagine it's possible in relation to a limited number of matters that we feel are important enough to justify that. But it's a matter I would invite parties to raise at a much later stage, once we've seen what particular places it would be appropriate to have a look at in the light of the evidence. Now, can I then deal with the other issues that each of you mentioned briefly before we rose. Mr. Hannis, you had something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, a couple things, Your Honour. One, can I touch on the site visit for a moment. I should tell Your Honour after the last 65 ter when we were advised by your Legal Officer that you had made a trip, I had written a letter to Defence counsel just asking if any of them had a problem with that, to advise me now rather than later, because in some jurisdictions that might be an argument. And Mr. Fila had responded that they didn't have any problem and proposed that we all make a site visit at some later date. Mr. Ackerman had written and said that he might have a concern, but I understand now he thinks it could be addressed if we all have a site visit at some later date. So I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was particularly carefully not to make it a visit for the purpose of looking at evidence, and as it turned out I landed up in Dubrava prison. I was released and can tell the tale. But there's absolutely no way in which what I saw there would have any bearing on an adjudication of the events in Dubrava prison. And as it turns out, it may be we'll never hear anything of them in any event. Apart from that I was in various communities and I did spend time in Pristina, but not in relation to looking at anything that might be relevant to the evidence. I just wanted a feel for what life in both Belgrade and Kosovo is like today because I thought it might help me when I came to listen to witnesses who come from the area and who may be influenced by conditions there at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One matter I wanted to raise relates to maps, Your Honour. We've put together a collection of Kosovo maps, Kosovo municipality maps, et cetera. We have enough to give one to each Defence team and for the Court. These are -- all have ERN numbers and are on our exhibit list. We would propose to hand those out at the beginning of the case and have them available for everybody, and if Defence counsel have any objection, we can certainly discuss that later on. But I wanted to bring that to your attention today and perhaps at the end of the session we can bring them down and hand them around to people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these better than the Kosovo atlases, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These are mostly drawn from the Kosovo atlas and they're blown up to be bigger to fit this size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other matter is something that related to a possible issue with the health of one of our accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We would like to go in private session, I think, to discuss that. The Defence counsel for that particular accused have asked that we go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to me that's an appropriate course unless anyone takes any objection. Generally speaking, in relation to matters of health, that would be appropriate. However, there are certainly exceptional circumstances in which even health ought to be a public issue, as you know. But in this situation then we should have private session. So can we please have private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, you had a matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. I must add something else that my colleagues have drawn my attention to. Could we perhaps receive from the Chamber an estimate on how much the case -- the trial would go on for, bearing in mind these new changes and amendments of the Prosecution case. Another thing that I wanted to say and I want to get this on the transcript just to make sure whether I understood what you previously said. Bearing in mind the motions we received from the OTP and the deadlines set for our reply, as well as the changes to the order of witnesses and any changes to the witness list, including some of the discussions we had at our 65 ter conferences with regard to the commencement of this trial and the schedule for the first week in July and the rest in August, I thought the summer recess would see the Defence teams working at full tilt to prepare for what comes next. That was my understanding of the period now stretching before us. I'm talking about the three weeks after the first recess. Our understanding is we have to forge ahead throughout this period of time in order to be ready for the continuation. At the same time, we have the schedule which leaves us with the obligation to prepare one of our motions during that period. If I could please have that confirmed so I can go back to the Registry and talk to them about how the Defence teams would be organising ourselves throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've understood the position correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as the first point is concerned about the estimate of the trial length, you can do this, I think, as well as me at the moment. But my rough calculation is that assuming there are no unforeseen interruptions, by the Christmas recess we shall have had about 400 hours. Now, that's intensive; I recognise that. But you've all along known my view that if we can apply ourselves intensively early in this case, it's going to give everyone a much better opportunity in the long run of preparing adequate submissions at the end of the trial. I don't think I'm breaking any confidences in telling you that so far as the Registry are concerned, when they look to me for an indication of the length of the case, I can't do better than tell them the Prosecution case shouldn't last more than a year. But I'm hoping, very hopeful, now that it's going to be significantly less than that. I find it impossible to judge the length of -- the likely length of the Defence case for reasons we discussed earlier in the hearing. But these are the vaguest of indications, and they depend on things going extremely well, and that's not really consistent with the history of this building. So I think that's as much as I am in a position to say to you today. But one thing that has happened today is that the Prosecution estimate of around 280 hours for the presentation of their evidence in chief must now be a bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be, but here's how it went. We had previously estimated 240 hours for examination-in-chief of our witnesses, with possibly another 40 hours for experts. If we don't lead evidence concerning the three municipalities that we've talked about, I'd have to tone up the hours for those witnesses, and we can subtract that number. However, the 92 bis witnesses we had not anticipated having any time for direct examination because we had the hope that they wouldn't come in. That's 56 witnesses, but any direct exam of them should be fairly short. And we're trying to do a number of our witnesses by 89(F). So maybe we're still at around the same figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm quite reassured by that, and I remain optimistic that things will get better. So these are very vague indications, but no one's in a position to do more than give that at this stage. Now, if that completes the issues that you wish to raise, then I just want very quickly to go through a number of points on which the Chamber is considering making an order giving guidance to parties on how proceedings should be conducted. Can I take it you have completed the various points that you wish to raise with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just conferred with Mr. O'Sullivan, and I don't think we should leave it to the Registry to decide on what the total time would be that would be required for the Prosecution case. We only have the Prosecutor's own estimate, and that still leaves time for cross-examination. I understand they can't be more specific now, or don't want to, but we do need some sort of a figure to face the Registry with. For us, this would be as good as a foundation for our case, and it also ensures that the standards of a fair trial are met. Maybe we don't need to have this right now, but we would appreciate having it over the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what do you think can be done more than to say to the Registry that the Prosecution case might take a year? I mean, that's the indication I've given, as requested, but I'm -- I still live in hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my omission. Thank you. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the matters that -- just in case there are comments the parties wish to make on these before the order is issued, I think we probably should set out for you the time-recording mechanism that will be used, because it's customary in these trials to record the time used by the various parties in presenting a case, and you should know in advance how that's being done, rather than simply have it given to you by surprise later. And I will set out that for you. Obviously, if anyone feels the need to make comments on orders of that nature which are issued, then you should make them sooner rather than later, but I suspect they won't be necessary because it's a practice that's a general practice followed in these cases. The intimation of documents which are going to be used in cross-examination, there should be a time set, a deadline set, for the intimation of the list of documents and the release of them through the e-court system. And that will be 24 hours prior to the anticipated start of the cross-examination of the witness, unless, Mr. Hannis, you want to make any comment about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That seems reasonable, and if there's an exceptional case, we'll address it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as exhibits are concerned, I have to confess having a little difficulty with the system that operates here of deciding specifically that something which has been understood to be a document that's in the case, as it were, or certainly in the files for the case becomes specifically exhibited after positive consideration being given to certain features. Now, that's a reflection of a rule about authenticity, probative value, and relevance. But it seems to me to take up an inordinate amount of time when there doesn't seem to be any issue over the document. So the practice we propose following is that when a party produces a document to a witness or in some other way, if no issue is taken with that, it will certainly become an exhibit in the case. It will be converted from a document that was in the parties' files to one of the exhibits in the case. And if there is any exception taken to it on any ground at all, then it's for the party to raise it at that stage. And the Bench will then have to make an adjudication on its admission. I expect you to either exercise discretion in this from the outset or, having had one or two rulings from the Chamber, to recognise what the practice is in relation to documents in general. Generally speaking, where you intend to rely on a book, then you should identify the parts of the book on which you rely; and the parts that the Trial Chamber will regard as evidence will be the parts which are featured in the exchanges between examining counsel and the witness. Similarly, with expert reports, the report will be admitted and considered by the Trial Chamber only to the extent that it's part of the evidence of the expert witness. Now, it may be the whole report, because the witness adopts the report and says, this is an accurate account of my findings in view of the investigations I've made. But there will be situations in which we decide that only parts of a report are going to be admitted in any event, and there will be others where only parts are relied upon by the parties. Hopefully untranslated documents in this case will be at a premium, but where they do arise, they will not be admitted until they are translated into the working language of the Court. We may issue more guidance on the use of Rule 89(F) and a little more guidance on hearsay, but we'll consider that and decide finally before this order is issued. I should say that the order will be available on Monday at the latest -- on Monday at some time before the evidence or at the time the evidence begins. Other Chambers may have made orders about the provision of 89(F) statements considerably -- a considerable period of time before the witness gives evidence. I think that's been done in the context of Rule 66(A)(i) regarding it as a disclosure question, but where the 89(F) statement is simply a rehash of material which has already been disclosed 66(A)(i) doesn't come into account -- or (A)(ii), rather, doesn't come into account. And we've discussed a system already for the production of -- or the production to the Defence of copies of the -- of the 89(F) statements. It may be that we should make a rule about that. The trouble about it is that some of the 89(F) statements may emerge from proofing, I suppose, or after proofing, and therefore they'll be pretty close. So we'll proceed on the basis that a minimum of 24-hour notice should be given, unless by agreement of the parties. As far as motions are concerned, we discussed the possibility of oral motions earlier. The order will probably make provision to clarify the situation where the Defence -- one of the Defence counsel makes a motion and others join in. We may set a time limit for that of seven days, and indeed where a response -- there's a response involved and they join in the response, we make a provision in relation to that. And that's to bring order to the situation, because there have been one or two examples in this case of rules about the time for responses not being observed. And it's important to bear these in mind. We're, generally speaking, inclined at the moment to have no regard to filings which don't comply with the rules. Now, unless there's any point arising in relation to these or you think there's another matter we should regulate -- Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps a point of clarification. On your first point regarding documents for cross-examination, my understanding that we are to provide those to the e-court system 24 hours before that witness testifies. But these items for cross-examination are not subject to disclosure to the Prosecution. Am I correct on that? They go into the system, but we're not disclosing it to the Prosecution prior to the witness's testimony because that would, I think, be contrary to the use we'd want to use these documents for during cross-examination, in issues of credibility or subject matter of their testimony. So I would submit that we put them into the e-court system for efficiency, but they aren't disclosed to the Prosecution before the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm thinking domestically rather than internationally at the moment, but the sort of document I would recognise as one which can be produced out of a hat, like a rabbit out of a hat, is one of which the witness inevitably has notice, in other words, something he may have written himself, used to challenge him. But if you are going to challenge one person's evidence by reference to something somebody else had prepared, another report or another account, that's something I would expect to be disclosed 24 hours beforehand, I think. Unless you can show to me that there's a different practice here. I'm not -- I'm not aware of a different practice, but that's probably my inexperience.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think the practice here is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's no requirement to disclose materials which we intend to use under Rule 90(H) in the cross-examination of a witness. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, are you saying that when it comes to the cross-examination by the Prosecution, that the same rule applies?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes. I may not know 24 hours in advance what my cross-examination of a witness will be. That may develop during that person's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now that's a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that's one of the situations. Another one may be I may have in mind, based on the out-of-court statement, matters I wish to test the evidence upon, and the statement may be going in one direction which I don't necessarily agree with or that I may want to test and I want to see what that witness has to say about that. And I don't think I should be giving that in anticipation of what he may or may not say on direct. And also for credibility. I don't see a situation, really, where I'm required to give advanced notice to the Prosecution of my line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sir, a comment. No, but then there is a type of documents where this is not required and what you're saying will be, to my mind, correct. You will not have to give a notice to the Prosecution about what those documents are going to be. Firstly, of which the witness is the author himself; secondly, a document which is prepared at the behest of the witness and he's supposed to be aware of it. But he will -- or he will never be confronted with a document which is just unknown to him or he has never been an author. If that is what you are thinking, then obviously you don't have to place in the hands of the Prosecution a document beforehand, obviously. In cross-examination, if you impeach the credibility of a witness. And if he's showing a document and you have another copy of it you can always confront. But it will not be every document for which the rule which is being very kindly proposed by you will be applicable. But it will be applicable where he is the author or where he has prepared the document or it has been prepared under his supervision. There will be no other document to that effect. And in that case, it's my personal view that you need not and you can bring out a document up your sleeves here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think Rule 90(H) answers the question, though, does it? Perhaps interpretation of it in cases may, but the rule itself doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's silent on the matter. In my submission, it's the nature of cross-examination itself which is such that -- there are other examples, Your Honour, that are -- well, a wide range of examples. There may be legislation which the witness can refer to, which he's not the author of but with which he's familiar. Your Honour has given me very specific examples, but there are others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, legislation is a public document. And a public document which has been -- like the gazettes one of your learned brothers here was mentioning. Those can be produced because they are public documents known to the public, and he can be confronted. No, that's always an exception. Include the public documents. Especially if it's legislation, well, then you can first ask him: Well, the legislation said this, and you were doing this; the rule said this, you were doing this; that's different. But normally the author's own document, but those are documents which are ipso facto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem, though, as I -- it's not in every jurisdiction that this form of ambush is permissible, but I see the problem where if you do it only 24 hours beforehand, what you do is you outline your cross-examination tactic. If, of course, you've done it long beforehand, along a list of other documents they're scattered through your 65 ter list in due course, then you don't disclose the line of cross-examination. So I understand the point, if you're only doing it at that time. The rule we would make would be designed to ensure the efficiency of our system here, and therefore, undoubtedly, you would have to have everything uploaded into the e-court system 24 hours beforehand. What I think we should do is consider what practice has been followed elsewhere and what rules there are before we make this determination. So I can assure you that we will review what practices have been followed elsewhere in this Tribunal before making a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: One final point. My understanding is the e-court system - and perhaps our friend from the Registry can help us - the e-court folder into which I would upload documents for cross-examination is a confidential folder between the Milutinovic team and the Registry. So that's not a problem. That's -- the whole point is that it remains in that folder and it's not shared with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that distinction. That's why I say that the real issue here is the notice you have to give to the Prosecutor. So that will be considered further, in the light of your submission. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's leave this problem about informing the Prosecutor aside for the time being. I'm just trying to imagine this possibility, bearing in mind the schedule and hearings that sometimes take all day. Let's imagine a witness who starts testifying one day and then soon after we move to our cross-examination. It's possible that during the chief some circumstances may arise requiring the Defence to react in a way which the -- has not been prepared. One thing I wanted to ask you is in your ruling today, please leave open a possibility for another way for the OTP or the Defence to introduce new documents, maybe not electronically if there's not enough time. These will be exceptional situations, but I think we should leave a possibility open for cases like these, the exception, not the rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you can take it that in relation to any matter of this nature on cause shown, the Court will depart from the strict terms of a rule. When we issue our order, if nothing is said on the matter it will be because we are undecided on it until the question actually arises. So the rule will -- the order will only cover matters that we think it's essential to deal with at this stage. Can I then -- Sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Just one short question, and it's, I think, very practical one. Can we confront the witness only with his previous statements or we can confront him with the statements of another witness's, for example, the Prosecutor's witnesses? If you find that some other witnesses talks completely different about the same issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Undoubtedly you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's all. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's perhaps a suitable occasion for me to indicate that you may want to make submissions about this if the situation arises, the concept of the hostile witness is not one that I'm terribly sympathetic to. It seems to me that a party should be entitled to examine a witness in the form that is appropriate to the circumstances. So if you bring somebody that turns out to be hostile to your case, I'm not, as presently advised, to demand that somehow or other you prove his hostility to the point where he has to be declared hostile before you start cross-examining him. I think under the proper control of the supervising court you should be allowed to examine witnesses as is appropriate. If that is of any assistance to you as a preliminary indication of what would happen without, obviously, finally deciding it, then please take account of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Trial Chamber would like to express their gratitude to counsel for the very helpful submissions that have been made throughout today's hearing, and we would like also to thank you for the cooperative way in which you have responded to the various requests we've made for assistance throughout the last week or so that this has been the Bench. And I personally would like to thank all counsel for their cooperation throughout the period that I've been the Pre-Trial Judge. That, effectively, brings the pre-trial proceedings, the active pre-trial proceedings in this case to an end. I now look forward to hearing all of you in the context of the trial. The indication from Mr. Hannis is that he might be something of the order of four hours, I gather, in his opening statement on Monday. We have an indication of somewhere between half an hour and an hour for the statement of Mr. Ojdanic. There is the possibility of evidence on Monday, but we'll deal with that as and when the situation arises. But I now adjourn this hearing and simply confirm that the trial ought to commence at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24
